Katalog Berita (Halaman 27/56)

#5950. Citi AAdvantage Executive Card Review: Better Lounges And More Status Credit

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

The Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] costs $695 a year, but I think it’s a better value today than it was at $595. American Airlines is investing seriously in its clubs again, and the card’s refresh added more credit towards elite status and benefits I can actually use.

I have the card. For a regular American Airlines flyer who wants Admirals Club access, it’s the place to start. The lounges are getting better, more are coming, and buying membership directly from American costs hundreds of dollars more.

When I covered the refresh, I thought the additional Loyalty Points alone justified the $100 annual fee increase for me. Citi has since added $200 in annual inKind dining credits, too.

The Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® includes full Admirals Club membership for the primary cardmember. American has priced standalone membership to make getting the card the obvious choice for someone eligible to apply. Here’s the current comparison: Option   Annual Cost   What You Get Citi AAdvantage Executive card   $695   Full membership, including guest privileges and eligible partner lounges Full membership bought from American   $1,200–$1,400, depending on status   Full membership, including guest privileges and eligible partner lounges Single membership bought from American   $750   Admirals Club access for the member, without guests or partner lounges Even an Executive Platinum member pays $1,200 for full membership. The card saves $505 before assigning any value to its miles, status bonuses or credits. Someone without status saves $705. And the card costs less than American’s restricted $750 membership option. There’s no annual visit allowance to ration and no spending requirement to unlock unlimited visits. Qualifying Citigold customers can receive a $145 annual relationship credit, reducing their cost further. What The Lounge Access Includes American has nearly 50 Admirals Clubs, with more than 60 partner lounges extending the membership’s reach. Under American’s access rules: You can visit Admirals Clubs on eligible same-day itineraries, including American Airlines and oneworld flights. You don’t have to buy the ticket with this card. You can bring two guests or your immediate family—a spouse or domestic partner and children under 18. Guests need eligible same-day boarding passes, too. The primary cardmember’s membership includes eligible partner locations, such as Alaska Lounges and Qantas Clubs. The flight requirements vary by partner. This doesn’t include Flagship Lounges or Flagship Dining. Executive Platinum status by itself doesn’t get you into Admirals Clubs on ordinary domestic trips. Neither does a typical domestic first class ticket. The card also has an unusually good deal for additional cardholders: $175 total for up to three authorized users, then $175 for each additional user. Use all three slots and that’s about $58 per person annually. Each authorized user can visit Admirals Clubs without you and bring their own eligible guests. They need their physical card, identification and an eligible same-day boarding pass. They get Admirals Club access, rather than full membership, so they don’t get the partner lounge benefit. For a family, $870 in total annual fees can cover a primary cardmember and three authorized users traveling separately, with guest privileges. That’s less than American charges one Executive Platinum member for standalone full membership. If you only want a few visits a year, the $350 annual fee Citi® / AAdvantage® Globe™ Mastercard® [See rates and fees] includes four annual Admirals Club passes. American Is Finally Building Clubs I Want To Spend Time In For years American underinvested in lounges. They closed clubs, and when they renovated others the result was often the institutional look I’ve called “modern hospital.” The newer design is a huge improvement. Washington National’s E concourse club, Denver, Newark and Philadelphia show where American is going: warmer wood, better lighting, comfortable seating and spaces that feel inviting. I like this aesthetic more than the newer United Clubs or Delta Sky Clubs. The food has improved, too. I still generally prefer Delta’s lounge food, but American has moved well beyond the old snacks-and-soup proposition. Their fall Admirals Club menus include beef barbacoa taco bars in Chicago, Denver and St. Louis; sesame orange chicken at several West Coast clubs and Phoenix; and Creole style chicken with white bean cassoulet at the New York and Newark clubs. I’ve covered American’s plan for a new, renovated or expanded lounge nearly every month, on average, over two to three years. That’s very different from what we saw for much of the past decade. Among the projects: Charlotte: A new Admirals Club exceeding 40,000 square feet, with showers and multiple bars and food stations. Dallas–Fort Worth: A 37,000 square foot Terminal C club, plus a Provisions location planned for Terminal F. Austin: A replacement club exceeding 12,000 square feet, with American’s first outdoor lounge terrace. Chicago, Nashville, Miami and Washington National: New or expanded clubs, including Chicago’s L concourse project and the refresh of National’s Concourse D club. There’s also the Provisions grab-and-go concept, already operating in Charlotte, with additional locations announced for New York JFK and Dallas–Fort Worth. Sometimes you want food to take to the gate more than you want a seat in a lounge. And the most valuable part of a club can still be its agents. I’ve written about the Austin agents who keep looking for better connections after I’ve left. Having someone help fix a disrupted trip can be worth more than everything you eat and drink in the lounge that year. The Initial Bonus And Who Can Get It The current public initial bonus is 80,000 AAdvantage miles after $8,000 in purchases within the first three months of account opening. The annual fee is $695. Those are redeemable miles. The initial bonus doesn’t count as Loyalty Points towards status, although eligible spending to earn it does. Under Citi’s terms, you aren’t eligible for the initial bonus if you’ve received an Executive card new account bonus within the past 48 months. The restriction also covers converting another Citi card into an Executive account when that other account earned a new account bonus within the last 48 months. Simply having a different AAdvantage cobrand card doesn’t disqualify you. Up To 40,000 Extra Loyalty Points Without Spending On The Card The card awards 10,000 additional Loyalty Points at each of four thresholds during the AAdvantage qualification year, which runs March through February: Account Reaches   Cumulative Executive Card Bonuses 50,000 Loyalty Points   10,000 Loyalty Points 90,000 Loyalty Points   20,000 Loyalty Points 165,000 Loyalty Points   30,000 Loyalty Points 240,000 Loyalty Points   40,000 Loyalty Points The last two bonuses were added in the refresh. You don’t have to earn the qualifying Loyalty Points by spending on this card. Flying, shopping portal earnings, hotel bookings and spending on other AAdvantage cards can get you there. The bonuses themselves count towards subsequent thresholds. Earn 80,000 Loyalty Points outside this benefit and the first two bonuses bring you to 100,000. For someone pursuing Executive Platinum, the card can supply 30,000 of the required 200,000 Loyalty Points. Earning 170,000 elsewhere gets you there. The fourth bonus comes after Executive Platinum, helping towards higher Loyalty Point Rewards: 210,000 earned elsewhere plus the four bonuses gets you to 250,000. This is why the Executive card can make sense alongside another AAdvantage card. I have the Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees], too, and its spending can help trigger these Executive card bonuses. Globe’s Flight Streak bonuses can also stack with them. The Credits That Help Pay For The Card The October inKind addition is especially useful to me. I already use inKind at restaurants I’d eat at anyway. Here’s how the recurring credits work: $200 inKind dining credit: $100 for January–June and $100 for July–December. Add the card and benefit in the inKind app, then apply the credit when paying a participating restaurant through the app. There’s no minimum spend, and you can use it across multiple checks. Unused credit doesn’t carry over. Tips aren’t covered, and authorized users share the account’s allocation. Up to $500 American Airlines Vacations credit: Up to $250 in each half of the calendar year. This covers eligible vacation packages and Experiences purchased through American Airlines Vacations. Packages require at least two travel components, such as a flight and hotel or flight and car. Up to $100 for inflight and eligible Admirals Club purchases: A calendar year statement credit for eligible purchases charged to the card. Club food and beverages qualify. The inflight benefit applies to eligible domestic American Airlines and American Eagle flights. I won’t value this at the full $100 because many of the drinks and snacks I’d otherwise buy are already included through my status or seat, but it can cover additional purchases for family or premium club drinks. Up to $120 for Avis and Budget: Each calendar year, for eligible prepaid rentals booked directly at avis.com or budget.com and charged to the card. Pay later reservations and bookings through other travel sites don’t qualify. Up to $180 in Lyft credits: Take three eligible rides paid with the card in a calendar month, then receive a $15 Lyft credit. The credit expires after 30 days. This improved from $10 to $15 per month, but three rides are still required. Starting February 1, 2027, Wait & Save rides won’t qualify. If inKind saves you $200 on dining you’d otherwise pay for, that leaves $495 of annual fee to justify with lounge access, status bonuses and the other benefits. One old benefit is being phased out: the $10 Grubhub credit per monthly billing statement. Accounts opened before August 23, 2026 retain it through August 31, 2027. New applicants don’t get it, and the old 25% inflight food and beverage rebate has ended (replaced by the annual $100 credit). Hotel, Rental Car And Airport Benefits The refresh also added Omni Champion status and the ability to earn an annual free night. Enroll in the status benefit before your stay, allowing up to 14 days for activation. Then complete a qualifying stay of at least two consecutive nights, booked directly with Omni in your name and paid with the Executive card. That earns 100 Omni Credits for a free night on a later stay, once per calendar year. Redeem within 12 months. Taxes and resort fees are included in the award. A two-night stay you were going to make anyway can produce a valuable additional night. You can also enroll in Avis President’s Club through August 31, 2028. This offers upgrades and other rental benefits, although it’s duplicative for members who already receive it by reaching 100,000 AAdvantage Loyalty Points. Other benefits include: First checked bag free on eligible domestic American Airlines itineraries for the primary cardmember and up to eight companions on the same reservation. You don’t have to pay for the tickets with the card. Priority check-in, priority security where available and Group 4 boarding for the primary cardmember and up to eight companions on the same reservation. Up to $120 towards Global Entry or TSA PreCheck every four years when you pay the application fee with the card. No foreign transaction fees and travel protections including trip cancellation and interruption, trip delay, lost baggage and rental car coverage for qualifying purchases. What I’d Actually Spend On The Card The earning rates are: 12 miles per dollar on eligible AAdvantage Hotels and AAdvantage Cars bookings. 4 miles per dollar on eligible American Airlines purchases. 1 mile per dollar on other eligible purchases. Eligible spending earns one Loyalty Point per dollar. The category bonuses don’t multiply that: a dollar of American Airlines spending earns four redeemable miles and one Loyalty Point from the card. AAdvantage Hotels can separately award miles and Loyalty Points for the booking itself. The 12-mile rate is a strong reason to use this card when booking through American’s hotel and rental car platforms. I’d also use it where payment is required to earn a credit or benefit. For everyday spending, the decision is how much the additional Loyalty Points help you. American lets card spending make a real contribution to status, but earning one redeemable mile per dollar means giving up the rewards another card would have earned. You can keep the Executive card for its clubs and milestone bonuses while putting spending on a different card. After $150,000 in purchases during a calendar year, eligible American Airlines purchases earn five miles per dollar for the rest of that year. I wouldn’t do that just to earn one additional mile per dollar on subsequent airfare. You don’t have to pay for the tickets with the card. Priority check-in, priority security where available and Group 4 boarding for the primary cardmember and up to eight companions on the same reservation. Up to $120 towards Global Entry or TSA PreCheck every four years when you pay the application fee with the card. No foreign transaction fees and travel protections including trip cancellation and interruption, trip delay, lost baggage and rental car coverage for qualifying purchases. What I’d Actually Spend On The Card The earning rates are: 12 miles per dollar on eligible AAdvantage Hotels and AAdvantage Cars bookings. 4 miles per dollar on eligible American Airlines purchases. 1 mile per dollar on other eligible purchases. Eligible spending earns one Loyalty Point per dollar. The category bonuses don’t multiply that: a dollar of American Airlines spending earns four redeemable miles and one Loyalty Point from the card. AAdvantage Hotels can separately award miles and Loyalty Points for the booking itself. The 12-mile rate is a strong reason to use this card when booking through American’s hotel and rental car platforms. I’d also use it where payment is required to earn a credit or benefit. For everyday spending, the decision is how much the additional Loyalty Points help you. American lets card spending make a real contribution to status, but earning one redeemable mile per dollar means giving up the rewards another card would have earned. You can keep the Executive card for its clubs and milestone bonuses while putting spending on a different card. After $150,000 in purchases during a calendar year, eligible American Airlines purchases earn five miles per dollar for the rest of that year. I wouldn’t do that just to earn one additional mile per dollar on subsequent airfare. For years American underinvested in lounges. They closed clubs, and when they renovated others the result was often the institutional look I’ve called “modern hospital.” The newer design is a huge improvement.

Washington National’s E concourse club, Denver, Newark and Philadelphia show where American is going: warmer wood, better lighting, comfortable seating and spaces that feel inviting. I like this aesthetic more than the newer United Clubs or Delta Sky Clubs.

The food has improved, too. I still generally prefer Delta’s lounge food, but American has moved well beyond the old snacks-and-soup proposition. Their fall Admirals Club menus include beef barbacoa taco bars in Chicago, Denver and St. Louis; sesame orange chicken at several West Coast clubs and Phoenix; and Creole style chicken with white bean cassoulet at the New York and Newark clubs.

I’ve covered American’s plan for a new, renovated or expanded lounge nearly every month, on average, over two to three years. That’s very different from what we saw for much of the past decade.

There’s also the Provisions grab-and-go concept, already operating in Charlotte, with additional locations announced for New York JFK and Dallas–Fort Worth. Sometimes you want food to take to the gate more than you want a seat in a lounge.

And the most valuable part of a club can still be its agents. I’ve written about the Austin agents who keep looking for better connections after I’ve left. Having someone help fix a disrupted trip can be worth more than everything you eat and drink in the lounge that year.

The current public initial bonus is 80,000 AAdvantage miles after $8,000 in purchases within the first three months of account opening. The annual fee is $695. Those are redeemable miles. The initial bonus doesn’t count as Loyalty Points towards status, although eligible spending to earn it does. Under Citi’s terms, you aren’t eligible for the initial bonus if you’ve received an Executive card new account bonus within the past 48 months. The restriction also covers converting another Citi card into an Executive account when that other account earned a new account bonus within the last 48 months. Simply having a different AAdvantage cobrand card doesn’t disqualify you. Up To 40,000 Extra Loyalty Points Without Spending On The Card The card awards 10,000 additional Loyalty Points at each of four thresholds during the AAdvantage qualification year, which runs March through February: Account Reaches   Cumulative Executive Card Bonuses 50,000 Loyalty Points   10,000 Loyalty Points 90,000 Loyalty Points   20,000 Loyalty Points 165,000 Loyalty Points   30,000 Loyalty Points 240,000 Loyalty Points   40,000 Loyalty Points The last two bonuses were added in the refresh. You don’t have to earn the qualifying Loyalty Points by spending on this card. Flying, shopping portal earnings, hotel bookings and spending on other AAdvantage cards can get you there. The bonuses themselves count towards subsequent thresholds. Earn 80,000 Loyalty Points outside this benefit and the first two bonuses bring you to 100,000. For someone pursuing Executive Platinum, the card can supply 30,000 of the required 200,000 Loyalty Points. Earning 170,000 elsewhere gets you there. The fourth bonus comes after Executive Platinum, helping towards higher Loyalty Point Rewards: 210,000 earned elsewhere plus the four bonuses gets you to 250,000. This is why the Executive card can make sense alongside another AAdvantage card. I have the Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees], too, and its spending can help trigger these Executive card bonuses. Globe’s Flight Streak bonuses can also stack with them. The Credits That Help Pay For The Card The October inKind addition is especially useful to me. I already use inKind at restaurants I’d eat at anyway. Here’s how the recurring credits work: $200 inKind dining credit: $100 for January–June and $100 for July–December. Add the card and benefit in the inKind app, then apply the credit when paying a participating restaurant through the app. There’s no minimum spend, and you can use it across multiple checks. Unused credit doesn’t carry over. Tips aren’t covered, and authorized users share the account’s allocation. Up to $500 American Airlines Vacations credit: Up to $250 in each half of the calendar year. This covers eligible vacation packages and Experiences purchased through American Airlines Vacations. Packages require at least two travel components, such as a flight and hotel or flight and car. Up to $100 for inflight and eligible Admirals Club purchases: A calendar year statement credit for eligible purchases charged to the card. Club food and beverages qualify. The inflight benefit applies to eligible domestic American Airlines and American Eagle flights. I won’t value this at the full $100 because many of the drinks and snacks I’d otherwise buy are already included through my status or seat, but it can cover additional purchases for family or premium club drinks. Up to $120 for Avis and Budget: Each calendar year, for eligible prepaid rentals booked directly at avis.com or budget.com and charged to the card. Pay later reservations and bookings through other travel sites don’t qualify. Up to $180 in Lyft credits: Take three eligible rides paid with the card in a calendar month, then receive a $15 Lyft credit. The credit expires after 30 days. This improved from $10 to $15 per month, but three rides are still required. Starting February 1, 2027, Wait & Save rides won’t qualify. If inKind saves you $200 on dining you’d otherwise pay for, that leaves $495 of annual fee to justify with lounge access, status bonuses and the other benefits. One old benefit is being phased out: the $10 Grubhub credit per monthly billing statement. Accounts opened before August 23, 2026 retain it through August 31, 2027. New applicants don’t get it, and the old 25% inflight food and beverage rebate has ended (replaced by the annual $100 credit). Hotel, Rental Car And Airport Benefits The refresh also added Omni Champion status and the ability to earn an annual free night. Enroll in the status benefit before your stay, allowing up to 14 days for activation. Then complete a qualifying stay of at least two consecutive nights, booked directly with Omni in your name and paid with the Executive card. That earns 100 Omni Credits for a free night on a later stay, once per calendar year. Redeem within 12 months. Taxes and resort fees are included in the award. A two-night stay you were going to make anyway can produce a valuable additional night. You can also enroll in Avis President’s Club through August 31, 2028. You cover all this, but I do think the updates to this card are excellent. Approaching Amex Platinum levels of refresh improvement.

– inKind is available in more places than you might expect. My local coffee shop is on inKind. My local pizza place is on inKind. Sure you can value the $200 at something less because of prepayment and because you can buy inKind giftcards for as low as $64.99 on Black Friday or whatever, but this is still as good as cash. This isn’t a Resy credit where you are likely sitting down for a meal, let alone a CSR OpenTable credit that’s available in tens of restaurants nationwide. The inKind credit covers lots of places that are on-the-go, picking up some pizza for dinner for the family on the way home types of charges. Even if you value the credit at only $130-150, it’s very cash-like in its use, and not illusory at all. And $100 every 6 months is 10x better than $10 a month at Grubhub.

– 20k more LPs is nothing to sneeze at, and also makes it much easier to get to the valuable 250k LP reward level. Would it surprise me if at some point soon AA raised the LPs required to reach status levels so that they align with when you get the 4x10k LP boosters? Nope.

– 12x versus 10x on AA Hotels / Cars is terrific! That’s an extra $3 in value per $100 spent (assuming you value a mile at 1.5cpm). And if you have any AA status, with any AA card, you are getting a good amount of additional base miles/LP on AA Hotels and Cars in addition to the 1x base/11x bonus miles you’re getting on spend. It’s not crazy to think that you might get an additional 15k base miles/LP for $1k of spend – the idea that you might get 27k miles (~$405 of value) and 16k LP on $1k of spend is a terrific return! And it’s 19.75k LP if you reached 60k LP and activated the 25% bonus on your LP through partners for a 6 month period. Basically half way to AA Gold on 1x$1k stay, and you’re getting an extra ~$30 in value per $1k (versus the previous 10x earning rate on AA Hotels).

-$100 inflight/club credit may not be that useful for solo flyers who are EP and get a free cheese plate already, but when traveling with the family – easy snacks to buy on board, the cost of which is now fully covered versus 25% off. Big improvement – unless you were already spending more than $400 a year on AA F&B on board (which seems unlikely for most people).

– Even if you value the AA Vacations credit at $0 (even with the current MaximizeMiles promotion I tend to think AA Vacations is more trouble than its worth given the restrictive cancellation policies plus the fact that you would likely earn more miles/LP booking your flight and hotel and car separately with AA / AA Hotels / AA Cars), AA/Citi are still delivering revised economics that more than offset the additional $100 AF.

Bottom line – this is a fantastic card refresh.

Are the loyalty points bonus thresholds retroactive? Meaning if I’ve already earned 100.000+ LPs for 2026 program year if I’m approved for the card will I “immediately” (or at least before Feb end) get the 20,000 point LP bonus?

“Up to $100 for inflight and eligible Admirals Club purchases:. … Club food and beverages qualify.”

Which clubs have did for purchase anymore? I’m the last 6 months I have tried BOS, LGA, CLT, ORD, DFW and none have food. Either the QR code only has drinks or I tried to order from the QR menu and was told they didn’t have any food anymore. I would often get a to go order from the lounge… Better than a sandwich from Hudson’s. The food at the lounge has improved, but it’s still less of a meal than what they had on the QR menu.

#5949. Spirit Airlines Shut Down—Did It Forget To Cancel Its Internet? Comcast Wants $1.25 Million

Spirit Airlines stopped flying in May, but Comcast and its subsidiaries say it still owes $1.25 million in internet bills. Some charges are for locations Spirit says it left in 2024—but the providers say they haven’t produced records showing the service was canceled. Always keep proof when dealing with Comcast! Part of this sounds like Spirit forgot to turn off its internet when it moved out. According to the providers, on October 22 the airline authorized them to disconnect every location except Dania Pointe in Dania Beach, Florida. That was nearly six months after the airline stopped flying. Their November 19 court filing asks the bankruptcy judge to order payment and make Spirit decide whether to keep or reject the contracts. Comcast and its Masergy subsidiary say some services were still running when they filed. Spirit shut down on May 2 after it couldn’t obtain the money to keep operating. No one would continue to fund its massive losses. But the bankruptcy process to unwind its business remains ongoing. There are assets to sell, contracts to resolve, records to maintain and creditors arguing over who gets paid. I’ve covered the lawsuit from workers seeking 60 days of pay over the abrupt shutdown and the court-approved $668 million sale of a 27-aircraft portfolio. Much of that aircraft price represented lenders applying what Spirit owed them toward their purchase. The four internet providers list these unpaid balances: Provider Amount Claimed Comcast Cable Communications Management $219,743.41 Masergy Cloud Communications $164,626.99 Masergy Communications $849,646.45 Nitel $11,990.73 Total $1,246,007.58 Comcast acquired Masergy in 2021 and Nitel in 2025. This is for internet service at Spirit locations, not inflight wifi (which was provided by Thales). The providers say they’ve repeatedly sought payment. Spirit responded that some locations had been vacated in 2024, and that disconnection requests should have been submitted for others. You might expect the internet companies simply to get in line with Spirit’s other unpaid creditors. For bills dating to before the bankruptcy, that’s probably what happens. But these companies say they continued providing services after Spirit filed on August 29, 2025. Necessary expenses of running a company in bankruptcy can qualify as administrative expenses, which get priority over other unsecured debts, or else no one would keep supplying a bankrupt business trying to turn itself around. And services needed to sell its assets and administer the remaining business can continue to qualify. It’s unclear what treatment will apply to internet Spirit was no longer using, even if it hadn’t cancelled the contracts. Comcast needs to establish the benefit their services supplied to the bankruptcy estate. In fact, their motion cites In re Enron but that denied administrative priority for unused pipeline capacity that hadn’t benefited the estate. Internet connections supporting the Spirit Airlines liquidation are likely to get repayment priority But defunct services that hadn’t merely been cancelled might not. A hearing is scheduled for December 16, with responses due December 9. And even a successful priority claim doesn’t necessarily mean Comcast gets immediate payment. In Midway Airlines, a telephone equipment lessor won an administrative claim for unpaid lease obligations, but the appeals court upheld making it wait for payment alongside other administrative creditors. So Comcast may have to wait as long for payment as you wait on hold to schedule a service appointment. Topics on this pageBankruptcyComcastSpirit AirlinesFlorida+1 more More From View from the Wing

#5948. A Swing Through Montana’s Art Treasures

Life on the range, Native spirits, Vienna, and Little Big Horn are pretty good raw material.

A “Greetings from Montana” postcard published by the E. C. Kropp Company, c. 1940.

Steven R. Shook Collection, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0

Today I’ll write about Big Sky Country — Montana. I’d never been. The Mountain States aren’t the place to go for Raphaels, Rembrandts, and Renoirs, but there are treasures to be found. What ought to be there? I very easily found my answer: Montana’s own Charles M. Russell, the perceptive, precise artist famous for his cowboy pictures but proudest of his scenes of Montana’s Chippewa, Blood Indian, and Lakota Natives. At 16, Russell (1864–1926) left school in Missouri to work on a sheep ranch in Montana. He lived under those spacious skies for the rest of his life, making thousands of works of art. A contemporary of Frederic Remington, he’s less known but just as good if not better.

Russell has a museum of his own in Great Falls, Mont., but he’s also got a suite of revelatory galleries at the Montana Heritage Center in Helena, my starting point as I explored the state from west to east. The Heritage Center, whose galleries are filled with art and artifacts from Montana’s Historical Society, opened late last year after a $160 million expansion and renovation. It’s wonderful. The Russell section is more or less chronological and a mix of art, hagiography, and atmosphere. I loved it. The entire new complex is great. It’s got a Russell section as well as multiple galleries on Montana’s history.

Brian T. Allen is National Review’s art critic.

On “A Swing Through Montana’s Art Treasures”

The Capital One Venture Business and Capital One Venture X Business appeal to business owners who don't want to turn every purchase into a strategy session. Both offer straightforward earnings, useful travel benefits and access to transferable miles. But with annual fees of $95 and $395, they have to clear very different bars.

Here's what each card delivers year after year so you can decide if your spending and travel habits make paying their respective fees realistic.

The Capital One Venture Business has a $95 annual fee, making it a low-maintenance option for business owners who want to earn travel rewards without committing to an expensive card. But although the fee is low enough to shrug off at first, it's not low enough to ignore indefinitely. The good news is it doesn't take much to break even.

New applicants can earn 100,000 bonus miles after spending $10,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, that bonus is worth $1,850. That takes care of the first-year math rather convincingly, with the card's recurring features giving you a reason to renew.

The 2-mile-per-dollar rate is the card's quiet strength. It's useful as a catch-all for your business spending, whether you're buying printer ink, a new laptop or 500 branded tote bags for a trade show. There are no categories to track and no earning limits to keep in mind.

The trade-off is that you won’t earn extra in categories where your business spends heavily, such as advertising or shipping.

That earning rate can cover the fee even if you ignore the credits. Based on TPG's valuation, 2 miles per dollar spent represents a 3.7% return. That valuation assumes you transfer your miles to airline and hotel partners rather than redeeming them at a flat 1 cent each.

Compared with a no-annual-fee card earning 2% cash back, you'd need roughly $5,600 in annual spending to make up the $95 fee from ongoing earnings alone.

One of my favorite things about the Venture Business is that it comes with credits that can potentially offset the annual fee. Each year, cardholders receive up to $50 back (as a statement credit) on purchases from qualifying advertising or software merchants and a $50 credit for bookings through Capital One Business Travel. Use both and the card pays for itself.

You can also get up to a $120 credit for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck every four years, Hertz Five Star status*, access to the Capital One Lifestyle Collection and no foreign transaction fees. None of those would sell the card on its own, but they’re nice to have.

Cardholders also get free employee cards, customizable spending limits and expense management tools that can be meaningful to a growing business.

*Upon enrollment, accessible through the Capital One website or mobile app, eligible cardholders will remain at that status level through the duration of the offer. Please note, enrolling through the normal Hertz Gold+ Rewards enrollment process (e.g. at Hertz.com) will not automatically detect a cardholder as being eligible for the program and cardholders will not be automatically upgraded to the applicable status tier. Additional terms apply.

The Venture Business is one of the easiest $95 decisions you'll make if you're a business owner who wants transferable miles and can naturally use at least one of its annual credits. Maybe you're running an online business, paying for monthly software subscriptions or spending money on advertising. You're already making those purchases, so you might as well earn miles along the way.

It's also a nice fit for someone who travels occasionally but doesn't necessarily need airport lounge access or a long list of premium travel perks.

If you want a simple earning structure, a manageable annual fee and flexible travel rewards, there's a lot to like about this card. But if you won't use those credits or transfer your miles, it's a tougher sell. In that case, a no-annual-fee card that earns cash back will probably do just as well.

To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Venture Business.

For business owners who travel regularly or put substantial spending on their cards, the Capital One Venture X Business offers a different kind of value. It has a much more noticeable $395 annual fee, but its value comes from a few large perks rather than a long list of small credits.

The card currently offers up to 300,000 bonus miles and a $1,000 Capital One Business Travel credit. New applicants earn 150,000 bonus miles after spending $40,000 on purchases within the first four months from account opening, plus another 150,000 bonus miles and the travel credit after spending $120,000 total during that period.

Based on TPG's valuations, the full 300,000-mile bonus is worth $5,550, before accounting for the $1,000 travel credit.

It's a spectacular first-year haul for a business that can comfortably meet the requirements. Still, the offer is enormous because the spending requirement is significant. If that isn't already in your business budget, don't stretch to hit it.

The Venture X Business is a pay-in-full card, meaning you should plan to pay the entire statement balance each month rather than paying over time with interest. Capital One may allow you to finance some purchases over time, but this isn't a good fit for a business that regularly needs more time to pay them off.

Like the Venture Business, this card shines at its base rate of 2 miles per dollar spent. It is particularly useful for large or irregular expenses that rarely fall into a traditional bonus category.

The portal rates add up if you book there regularly, though. If your business books $2,000 a year in hotels through Capital One Business Travel, that's 20,000 miles on the Venture X Business, compared with 10,000 on the Venture Business, or an extra $185 in value based on TPG’s valuations.

After the first year, the card's value rests largely on three recurring benefits:

Based on TPG's valuation, the bonus miles are worth $185, so the travel credit and anniversary miles alone cover the $395 fee. In that case, lounge access becomes additional value rather than something you need to count to justify the fee. It's all refreshingly clean math for a premium travel rewards card.

Other benefits include up to a $120 Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit, Hertz President's Circle status**, no foreign transaction fees and access to Capital One's Premier and Lifestyle hotel collections.

Another interesting feature is that Venture X Business has no preset spending limit. Your available purchasing power adjusts based on factors such as spending and payment history, which can be useful for businesses with larger or fluctuating expenses.

**Upon enrollment, accessible through the Capital One website or mobile app, eligible cardholders will remain at that status level through the duration of the offer. Please note, enrolling through the normal Hertz Gold Plus Rewards enrollment process (e.g. at Hertz.com) will not automatically detect a cardholder as being eligible for the program and cardholders will not be automatically upgraded to the applicable status tier. Additional terms apply.

I can see the Venture X Business being especially appealing to business owners who travel frequently, whether for conferences, client meetings or personal trips funded by the miles they earn.

If you're regularly booking flights and hotels, the annual travel credit, elevated travel rewards and lounge access can be genuinely useful.

It’s a harder sell if you prefer to book travel directly, rarely travel or sometimes need to carry a balance.

To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Venture X Business.

Both cards earn Capital One miles, so redeeming them works the same way no matter which card you have. You can keep things simple or put in a little more effort for the chance at greater value.

The easy option is to redeem miles at 1 cent each, either to cover travel you’ve already charged to the card or to book through Capital One Business Travel. That gives purchases earning 2 miles per dollar spent a dependable 2% return toward travel.

For me, transfer partners are what separate these cards from ordinary cash-back options. Transfers can push the return well beyond 2%, especially when cash fares are expensive or premium-cabin award space is available.

And there's plenty of flexibility: Capital One has more than 15 travel transfer partners, including programs like Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France-KLM Flying Blue, British Airways Club and Wyndham Rewards.

For example, 50,000 miles can cover $500 in eligible travel charges. But transferring the same balance to book an Iberia business-class award from Chicago to Madrid could save $2,500 or more, as just one example. That distinction matters when evaluating the annual fees since Capital One miles only beat cash-back credit cards if you intend to transfer miles to partners.

Capital One lets you move miles between your business and personal cards, making it easy to pool them before booking a big award.

Both cards have a lot going for them, especially if you're interested in earning straightforward transferable miles on everyday business spending.

The Venture Business card has a low annual fee with practical credits that can offset the annual fee, and its everyday earning and redemption rates match those of the pricier Venture X Business.

If you'll use the $300 travel credit, the Venture X Business is a better deal, even at more than four times the price. It tacks on anniversary miles and lounge access that add value to frequent flyers while maintaining the simplicity and flexibility of flat-rate travel earnings.

And if you don’t plan to transfer miles to airline or hotel partners, a no-annual-fee cash-back card may be all you need.

Learn more: Capital One Venture X Business

#5945. Hilton Diamond Guest Says He Gets Sent Next Door For Coffee—And Treated Like He Was Stealing Breakfast

I’ve written about people walking into hotels where they aren’t staying and helping themselves to a full breakfast. Somehow getting an actual guest a cup of coffee can be more complicated.

John Konrad’s account of the coffee dispute, November 21, 2026

In the second half of the thread, the manager talks up Homewood’s overnight oats. Konrad decides he’d like some after all. He’s refused because he’s registered next door. He raises his voice, objects to being told to calm down (no one in history has ever calmed down because they’ve been told to calm down), and eventually refuses an offered gym pass.

I AM A DIAMOND MEMBER BEING CROSS-EXAMINED OVER CHIA SEEDS.

The replies include plenty of people who think he’s being insufferable. One person who says they’ve stayed at both properties reports that guests routinely move between them. When a critic calls him a Karen, Konrad points back to his Curb Your Enthusiasm framing making himself part of the joke.

The two hotels have shared ownership by the Mian Companies. Signs direct Hilton Garden Inn guests to Homewood’s gym during construction. Homewood Suites Oxnard/Camarillo includes breakfast for its guests. Hilton Garden Inn has a different model. In the United States, eligible Gold and Diamond members who select the benefit receive a $10 daily food and beverage credit per person, for up to two registered guests. And asking for a room number when someone complains about a key is normal. A hotel employee can help with access. But a staff referral should make getting coffee easy. If the two hotels haven’t agreed on what guests can use, they need to sort that out between themselves. Meanwhile, People Really Do Walk Into Hotels For Free Breakfast I’ve covered people walking into a Drury Inn just to eat and people stopping at hotels for breakfast on their way to work. At many limited service properties, nobody checks. Looking comfortable in the lobby can be enough. At the aloft Dallas Love Field in 2022, I selected breakfast as my Marriott elite welcome amenity instead of 500 points. The Aloft and Element occupied the same building, with separate entrances. Breakfast meant walking over to the Element’s lobby buffet, which was included for guests staying there. Nobody asked my name, room number, or whether I’d selected breakfast. I could have taken the points and eaten anyway. Someone who wasn’t staying at either hotel could have walked in just as easily. This favors people who look like they belong. Konrad adds that he hadn’t shaved and his clothes were stained from boat work. He thinks that may explain some of the suspicion. There are real costs to feeding people who aren’t guests. There are also costs to policing breakfast: staff time, lines, and embarrassing the customers who are supposed to be there. A hotel can spend more trying to prevent a small loss than the food would have cost, especially if it chases away repeat business. Hotels Keep Getting Coffee Wrong I’ve been writing about the importance of hotel coffee for years. A business hotel ought to have drinkable coffee available around the clock, with real milk or cream. Guests arrive from other time zones, wake up early for flights, and get up before dawn to work. Their day have to start when the restaurant opens. At what was then the W San Diego, I was staying in the Extreme Wow suite. Still on East Coast time, I woke around 4:30 a.m. At about 5 I called the Whatever/Whenever line for coffee. They told me it wasn’t available until 6. They couldn’t provide whatever (coffee) whenever (in the morning). I wound up walking to Starbucks. I’ve also written about: The then-Andaz Wall Street removing its 24 hour lobby coffee, when rooms didn’t have coffee machines and room service wasn’t available around the clock. Hyatt Herald Square’s coffee stand opening 30 minutes late. Park Hyatt Washington offering 24 hour room service, but refusing overnight coffee. There was a Starbucks across the street there, too. And I don’t love Starbucks, they’re simply ubiquitous. And then there’s the time the Sheraton Macao investigated me for trying to steal coffee. I ordered six cups from room service. After pouring two, the pot was nearly empty. I called down, and they agreed to send four more. Instead, at 6:30 a.m. the delivery employee appeared at my door and announced: I am here to investigate. He insisted the machine was electronic, so it couldn’t have dispensed too little. Then he poured out what remained. Half a cup. There I was in my bathrobe, establishing that six cups and two and a half cups weren’t the same thing before he’d hand over the replacement coffee he’d already brought upstairs. Starwood apologized and offered 5,000 Starpoints. I declined. The hotel’s in-room dining manager apologized as well. They’d turned a short pot of coffee into a staff investigation, a corporate response, and an offer of points. Bringing the coffee would have been cheaper. And asking for a room number when someone complains about a key is normal. A hotel employee can help with access. But a staff referral should make getting coffee easy. If the two hotels haven’t agreed on what guests can use, they need to sort that out between themselves.

As one of the world's largest cruise ships, Royal Caribbean's Legend of the Seas promises no shortage of things to see, do and eat. With an expansive lineup of dining and entertainment venues, pools and activities, there's enough onboard to fill an entire vacation without ever stepping off the ship.

But as someone without extensive cruising experience, I boarded the ship with a few preconceived notions about what the rooms, crowds and restaurants would be like.

After sailing on the ship's inaugural voyage, however, I found myself pleasantly surprised by several aspects of the experience. Here are five things I didn't expect.

With thousands of passengers on board, I expected finding a place to lounge by the pool, grab a drink or simply sit and relax to be a bit of a challenge. After all, even the largest cruise ship in the world has a finite amount of space.

Given that the ship's double-occupancy capacity is 5,610, I was surprised by how rarely I felt surrounded by crowds.

I was traveling with a friend, and we could almost always find available lounge chairs; we rarely encountered long lines at restaurants, bars or other public areas. Elevators were easy to navigate, and I never felt like I was constantly waiting behind a crowd of other passengers.

There were a few exceptions. Some of the pools got busy, and popular performances and events filled up quickly, so planning ahead was important if I wanted to see something specific. But even during popular moments, like the rooftop deck fireworks display, there was enough room to enjoy the show without feeling packed in.

The same was true during our visit to Perfect Day at CocoCay, Royal Caribbean's private island in the Bahamas. We spent time at South Beach and Cove Beach, where there were plenty of open spots to settle in and enjoy a peaceful vibe.

For a ship carrying so many passengers — up to 7,600 passengers at maximum capacity — I was surprised by how easy it was to find a little breathing room.

Related: The ultimate guide to Royal Caribbean cruise ships and itineraries

Cruise lines aren't shy about advertising their entertainment, but I wasn't entirely sure what to expect from the actual productions. I figured there would be plenty of activities to keep passengers occupied, but I didn't anticipate the caliber of performances I saw onboard.

The AquaTheater show was one of the highlights of my sailing. The production featured acrobatics, high dives and aerial stunts that had the audience audibly gasping throughout the show.

The ice skating production Fusion was another standout. The performers were incredibly talented, and the show was engaging from beginning to end. There was also a full production of “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory” that I unfortunately didn't have time to see.

Beyond the major productions, there was plenty of entertainment to stumble upon throughout the ship. The live music was consistently good, and we happened upon a silent disco where passengers of all ages were dancing while listening to music through their own headphones.

We also participated in an onboard escape room, which was just as thoughtfully designed and challenging as some of the escape rooms I've experienced on land.

I went into the sailing thinking of entertainment as something to do between meals and pool time. Instead, it became one of the reasons I was excited to explore the ship.

Related: The 7 classes of Royal Caribbean cruise ships, explained

I knew Legend of the Seas would have plenty of dining options, from casual restaurants to more upscale specialty dining. But I wasn't expecting one of my favorite experiences of the entire sailing to be an eight-course tasting menu at the Old Hollywood Supper Club.

The experience felt completely removed from the typical cruise-ship dining environment. The restaurant's glamorous old Hollywood decor, live musical quartet and immersive atmosphere made dinner feel like an evening out in its own right.

The eight-course menu was thoughtfully presented, with each dish accompanied by a corresponding cocktail. Our servers were incredibly knowledgeable about the food and drinks, and there were little surprises throughout the meal, including an amuse-bouche to start and an unexpected dessert at the end.

Some highlights included blinis with caviar and goat cheese, which came paired with what the restaurant called a Sunset Martini, and the wagyu filet, which was paired with the club’s version of an Old Fashioned. Even the palate cleanser — a vodka-infused sorbet presented theatrically under a smoky glass top — was well thought out and delicious.

It was a three-hour dining experience with enough time to enjoy each course, discuss all the flavors with my tablemates, enjoy the live music (which included songs that coincided with each course) and get excited about what was coming next in the story. For a few hours, I almost forgot I was eating aboard a cruise ship.

I assumed this ship would have plenty of casual, approachable, kid-friendly dining options (which it did), but this experience made me realize there are also opportunities for a more sophisticated night out onboard.

With so many restaurants, bars, pools, entertainment venues and distinct neighborhoods, I assumed it would take me a while to get my bearings on Legend of the Seas. But the ship's size never felt overwhelming, and I found it surprisingly easy to navigate. Clear signage made it simple to find my way between venues, elevator displays helped me figure out where I needed to go, and crew members were always nearby if I had a question.

That ease extended beyond the ship itself. The Wi-Fi connection was strong enough that I could research the different beaches and amenities at Perfect Day at CocoCay before we arrived, making it easy to plan how I wanted to spend my day. Once ashore, complimentary trams made it simple to get between different areas of the island without having to walk everywhere.

For a ship with so much happening at once, I appreciated how little effort it took to get where I wanted to go and make the most of my time.

Related: The best Royal Caribbean cruise ship for every type of traveler

Before this sailing, I had always pictured cruise ship cabins as fairly cramped spaces with just enough room for a bed and a small bathroom. I expected to spend most of my time out exploring the ship and very little time actually enjoying my room.

My cabin on Legend of the Seas changed that perception.

I stayed in a Spacious Infinite Ocean View Balcony Room, which had a large bed, a couch and a sitting area by the floor-to-ceiling window. There wasn't a true balcony, but the sitting area and full floor-to-ceiling window gave a balcony-like feel. Guests in these rooms can open and close the windows using a button on the side of the window.

There was a surprising amount of storage available in the room. Between the full closet, dresser drawers and bathroom shelves, there was plenty of room to unpack and keep everything organized rather than living out of a suitcase. There was also enough space for two people to get ready without constantly maneuvering around each other.

Of course, a cruise ship cabin isn't going to offer the same square footage as a traditional hotel room. But I was impressed by how thoughtfully the space was laid out and how comfortable it felt for two people.

#5942. Trump banks on personal relationships moving Putin, Xi toward U.S. interests

Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump arrive for a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. (Win McNamee/AFP via Getty Images)

That was the greeting, complete with a lengthy handshake, President Donald Trump gave Vladimir Putin before two high-level meetings Thursday, including the first “trilateral” session with sitting U.S., Russian and Chinese heads of state.

“It’s nice to see you,” Trump told Putin before a private one-on-one meeting in China’s Shenzhen economic zone, before pulling the Russian strongman close and saying something into his ear too low for journalists’ microphones to pick up.

Trump and Putin then posed for the cameras with wide grins, again underscoring the U.S. president’s closeness with a world leader who has been partially shunned by the West since he launched a war with Ukraine in February 2022. Trump on Thursday also appeared several times alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping, who like Putin has been scorned by Republican and Democratic lawmakers for years.

“We’ve had a great relationship for many years. We've known each other for a long time. And I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this — or, at least, start,” Trump told reporters as Putin beamed from a few feet away.

They later were joined by Xi for a group photo before sitting down at a round wooden table with a large arrangement of pink flowers in the center.

His interactions with and comments about Putin and Xi reflect Trump’s belief that his personal relationships can bend them toward U.S. interests. But that gambit clashed Thursday with his second term’s expiration date — the White House did not disclose any agreements reached during his various meetings with the two leaders, nor did Trump hold a press conference following the three-way session.

Both Putin and Xi are adept at playing the geopolitical long game. The 26 months left in Trump’s term is a relatively short amount of time compared to the duo that has been in power for a combined 56 years and will remain in place for the foreseeable future.

Indeed, even Trump acknowledged the first-ever meeting might not immediately yield much progress on its ostensible goal: paring each powers’ nuclear weapons arsenals.

“I must say, it's, quite frankly, a very hard thing to do, because once you have the nuclear weapons, it's very hard to not have them. It's very hard to give them up as the leader of a country,” Trump said as Putin and Xi looked on. “Something that's very difficult to say, because … it's the way life works.

“You know, you have thousands of weapons and you're supposed to give them up, and yet you have countries in addition to us, in much smaller numbers, but they have nuclear weapons, also,” he added. “So it's not an easy thing to do and give them up.”

Trump, who was convicted by a New York jury in a business records case and who saw a federal election interference case against him dismissed only because of his reelection, also appeared to join Putin’s resistance to international criminal justice entities that have alleged Putin has committed war crimes in Ukraine.

“In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nations’ sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction,” Trump said, a statement that would be almost unthinkable to hear from any other sitting U.S. president.

Other world leaders, including democratically elected ones, at two Pacific region economic summits in which Trump participated this week did not receive the kind of cordial and personal treatment from the U.S. side that Putin and Xi enjoyed.

And other world leaders and congressional Democrats this week expressed concern with Trump's closeness to the Russian and Chinese strongmen.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., on Thursday called the unprecedented summit a “historic embarrassment.” He criticized Trump for leaving the meeting without any apparent concrete commitments from Moscow or Beijing on a number of issues, including curbing Chinese espionage inside U.S. companies and ending the Ukraine conflict.

“This summit was nothing but a glorified photo op and a gift to Putin and Xi,” Schumer said.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote this Thursday on X, shortly after Trump’s warm greeting for the former KGB officer: “God, protect us from such friends.”

Nicolas Burns, a former senior U.S. diplomatic official under GOP and Democratic presidents, was critical of Trump’s meetings with Xi. He said it was “important” for U.S. and Chinese leaders to hold talks, but added: “We need stability in the relationship with China — but there’s a but.”

“The president seems to be following a detente policy with China, with very little substance. There’s a lot of pomp and circumstance, red carpets, a lot of nice words,” the former ambassador to China, NATO and Greece told “Morning Joe” on MS NOW. “Too friendly with Xi Jinping, who’s not going to be swayed by rosy words from President Trump.”

Even before Trump met with the Russian and Chinese leaders behind closed doors, Republican and Democratic lawmakers said they doubted very much would come from it.

“I want nuclear weapons to be reduced. As you know, China has been unwilling to even have a conversation with the United States about nuclear arms reduction until they reach a certain plateau in the number of weapons that they have,” House Armed Services Committee Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., told reporters Tuesday.

“I'm glad that they're willing to have the conversation. We do need a limit, as you know,” added Wittman, who lost his reelection bid earlier this month. “Right now, neither Russia nor China has a nuclear arms reduction treaty with the United States. It would be nice for us to actually have one.”

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., an Armed Services Committee member, wanted Trump to press Putin over Ukraine.

“Ukraine is defending itself from Putin's aggression, which this president should be opposing as well,” Blumenthal said Tuesday. “We are spending no money on Ukraine. Let's be very clear: Arms to Ukraine are purchased by Ukraine with financial support from Europe, not America. … Let's support Ukraine.”

On spending, Trump and administration officials have been pressing Senate Republicans to quickly pass another budget reconciliation measure with $350 billion more for the Defense Department. However, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and other GOP senators have signaled in the last 24 hours that they had shelved the notion of another fast-track spending measure.

“You have to have a path forward. You've got to get on it, and you have to protect it, and that takes 50 in the Senate,” Thune told reporters Thursday. “And then you've got to get it through the House. As you probably saw yesterday, a lot of folks in the House were lobbing grenades at the Senate reconciliation bill and complaints about it not being offset, et cetera. So, you know, in my view at least, you want to have a path forward to success.”

John M. Donnelly and Jackie Wang contributed to this report.

#5941. Accor’s Largest Shareholder Moves to Oust CEO After Ennismore Buyout

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Interior of Mama Shelter, Dijon.  Ennismore

Parvus, an activist investor, has criticized Accor's Ennismore buyout and 13 years of alleged stock price underperformance under CEO Sébastien Bazin. Accor's management has its own side to the story.

Accor’s largest shareholder, Parvus Asset Management, said Thursday it will ask shareholders to remove Sébastien Bazin as chairman and CEO at the hotel group’s next annual meeting, citing Accor’s €1.6 billion (about $1.8 billion) buyout of its partners in its Ennismore joint venture and years of lagging returns.

Parvus, which holds about 14.1% of Accor’s share capital, worth about €1.6 billion, laid out its case in a letter published Thursday. Accor’s annual meetings are typically held in May, but the next date hasn’t been set.

Accor didn’t respond to Skift’s request for comment.

Parvus argues Accor has long underperformed its peers. “Accor shares have returned 99% from December 2013 to November 2026, against 593% for IHG, 863% for Hilton, and 950% for Marriott,” it wrote. “In our view, this sustained gap reflects an unfocused strategy, inconsistent capital allocation, and inadequate governance oversight.”

Parvus Asset Management, Accor's largest shareholder with about 14.1% of share capital, said Thursday it will ask shareholders to remove Sébastien Bazin as chairman and CEO at the group's next annual meeting, typically held in May. In a published letter, Parvus cited Accor's €1.6 billion ($1.8 billion) buyout of its minority partners in the Ennismore lifestyle joint venture and a long stretch of lagging returns, noting Accor shares returned 99% from December 2013 to November 2026 against 593% for IHG, 863% for Hilton, and 950% for Marriott. Bazin countered on Accor's analyst call that the €3.7 billion equity value for Ennismore came from a formula written into the 2022 shareholders' agreement, not from negotiation this week, and that the 2022 sale proceeds funded a buyback and special dividend that amounted to "basically a 2x return" for shareholders. Accor will buy the 44.3% minority stake in three tranches through January 2028, funded in rough thirds from non-core asset sales, new debt, and cash or shares. Bazin said he struggles to see Accor holding 100% of Ennismore over the medium to long term and that an IPO is still possible. Accor didn't respond to Skift's request for comment.

Why was Xi blocking the exported chips the Trump administration was willing to give him?

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and an Nvidia AI chip

Why wasn’t China taking the chips? The ones President Trump was willing to sell them — for a piece of the action, naturally. The ones Xi Jinping didn’t need to steal.

The question presents, for me, another valuable lesson in humility — in what Rich Lowry and I discussed on our podcast this week as the imperative of checking your premises when real-world events pose unexpected complications.

Andrew C. McCarthy is a senior fellow at National Review Institute, an NR contributing editor, and author of Ball of Collusion: The Plot to Rig an Election and Destroy a Presidency.

#5939. The House has a new lame-duck challenge: Attendance

House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., pictured at the U.S. Capitol on Thursday, said attendance is 'a great frustration.' (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Republicans who want to accomplish as much as possible before Democrats take control of the House are confronting a new challenge: Attendance.

Thirty-two members – 21 Republicans, 10 Democrats, and one independent – did not vote in Thursday morning’s session before members headed out of town a day early for Thanksgiving break. This, a day after House GOP leadership pulled a procedural rule vote when it was clear the vote might fall short because of GOP no-shows – and then canceled a planned Friday voting session.

The House has just 12 scheduled voting days left in the 119th Congress. And leaders who have at times struggled to ensure sufficient support for their agenda from the narrow majority now say they will work to make sure cases of senioritis don’t compound the problem, as both returning and nonreturning members have been part of the problem.

"Attendance is a great frustration for me right now,” House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., told reporters Thursday. “We'll be addressing that with members."

“We want to run through the tape and finish strong, but we can't do that unless people are present at work, so that's our challenge,” Johnson continued.

Of 13 roll call votes in the House since the midterms, all but one has had a double-digit number of no-shows; for five of the 13, more than 30 members did not vote. The average number of members not voting has more than doubled since the midterm elections, compared to the final 13 roll call votes beforehand.

Johnson has just a few more weeks before he steps out of the spotlight and Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, takes over the GOP conference as minority leader. But his members are still counting on him to get them back to Washington.

“I think there's going to be some serious conversations over the phone, behind the scenes over the weekend,” Rep. Michael Cloud, R-Texas, said. “We all took an oath of office. We have a sworn duty to be here. We're still being paid to be here, and you have to show up and do the job.”

And it's not just leadership that's frustrated with their missing colleagues this week.

“There is, no question,” Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., who narrowly won reelection, responded when asked whether there was frustration in the caucus over members' absences.

“I don't know what you do with people that don't understand the concept of duty,” Harrigan said. “I mean, look, you signed up for a two-year term. You execute your two-year term, no matter what happens along the way politically. You have an obligation both to your constituency and to your country to be here, so the fact that they're not self-motivated to be here, I don't think that there's really much that you can do.”

Attendance has also been a bipartisan problem. A group of House Democrats, including members of leadership, faced harsh criticism from party activists for not returning to the chamber in time for a vote related to a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

While Republican leadership grapples with the fallout from the party’s election losses earlier this month, lawmakers still face a slew of legislative items as Congress looks ahead to the holidays and a government shutdown looms.

Many Republicans want to see a party-line defense spending bill cross the finish line, while the NDAA remains in treacherous territory and Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act has been dark for months.

However, the frustration does not lie solely with absent House members.

“The Senate needs to do their job,” Rep. John McGuire, R-Va., said. “I know we had a hard time in the midterms. History doesn't favor the party in the president's office, but we passed the Save America Act five times here. It goes over there, nothing. We've got a farm bill, nothing. We got an NDAA. We got so many things.”

#5936. Populism Isn’t Built for Setbacks

The competitive advantage of conservatism over populism is that we are prepared for the inevitability of defeats.

President Donald Trump departs the White House, July 15, 2025, and supporters gather for a midterm campaign rally in San Antonio, Texas, October 7, 2026.

NR Illustration; Jonathan Ernst, Callaghan O’Hare/Reuters

Populism, for all of its faults, can be a powerful force in politics when it is rising. While populist agendas can come in many different varieties, they are all propelled by a broad sense that the people — or more properly, The People — are being held back by some elite force, whether that be Big Business or an insular political establishment or something darker. If only we can overcome the enemy, we are told, we will sweep to victory on the broad, sunny uplands.

As I’ve noted before, the very nature of populism is that it has to redefine The People to include something less than all the people when it inevitably encounters the reality that its premises are not universally shared. And so it goes from there, because populism always sooner or later must decide to cling to its narratives when forced to choose between them and empirical reality:

NR Illustration; Jonathan Ernst, Callaghan O’Hare/Reuters

Mr & Mrs Smith, the boutique hotel booking site Hyatt bought for £58 million ($72 million) in June 2023, grew volume sharply in 2025 but made less money on each booking, and its UK company posted a loss. Smith Global handled 209,565 bookings, up 41%, with more than half coming from World of Hyatt members, according to accounts filed with Companies House. Total booking value rose 19%, meaning the average booking fell about 16% to roughly £633 ($842), and the share Smith kept per booking dropped to about £112 from £139. Revenue grew 14% to £23.4 million while cost of sales rose 57%, pushing gross margin down to 67% from 76% and producing an operating loss of £1.5 million and a £2.7 million loss after tax. The directors said the mix of booking channels continued to place pressure on profitability. Hyatt's chief commercial officer Mark Vondrasek called the business "a strong success," citing access to European destinations where Hyatt has had limited brand presence, more than three-quarters of Smith bookings through Hyatt channels coming from elite members, and a doubling of World of Hyatt's share of luxury room nights in Europe, the Middle East and Africa. Hyatt recorded a $38 million goodwill impairment in its distribution segment in 2024 — the same amount as the goodwill booked on the deal — and has not said which business the charge related to. Hilton took a different route, licensing rather than buying with its Small Luxury Hotels of the World loyalty deal. Co-founder Tamara Lohan now oversees luxury across all of Hyatt.

#5934. Appeals court stands by LaMonica McIver ruling

Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., is seen on Capitol Hill last December. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., faced a setback Thursday in her effort to ditch charges tied to a scuffle during an oversight visit at an immigration detention facility last year, as a federal appeals court declined to reconsider its decision to let the case move forward.

The decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit leaves in place a 2-1 opinion from August which held that McIver was not immune from the charges, which stemmed from a confrontation between visiting members of Congress and federal agents while at the Delaney Hall facility in Newark. McIver has challenged the charges, arguing that her visit fell under the “speech or debate” immunity she has as a member of Congress because she was there to inspect detention conditions.

In a statement McIver said she and her attorneys were looking at “every possible option” in response to the appeals court ruling. Her statement invoked the Trump administration’s threats to treat oversight efforts as criminal conduct and said “we are all one step closer to a world in which the president of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for.”

“Donald Trump continues to send warning shots to Democrats in Congress and in all levels of power — but their case against me right now, in broad daylight, goes well beyond a warning. Because of a weaponized Department of Justice and because I dared to do my job and conduct oversight of ICE, I am facing 17 years in prison,” McIver said in her statement.

Following Thursday’s decision on rehearing, McIver could next ask the Supreme Court to weigh in on the case.

The August majority opinion from Judge Cindy Chung, which Thursday’s decision leaves in place, said that two of the three charges against McIver did not fall under the immunity, which is limited to legislative acts. The majority sent the third charge back to the lower court for another ruling.

“We have considered the ‘nature’ of the charged conduct and concluded it is unambiguously non-legislative,” the judge wrote.

Separately, Judge Thomas Ambro partially dissented to offer a different approach to the case. Ambro would have required the trial judge to more closely examine the exact conduct McIver was charged with, as well as to examine whether the Trump administration targeted her because of her political views.

“I would allow her discovery into the truth of the matter — not only for her own sake but to safeguard the independence of our legislative bodies,” Ambro wrote.

Ambro did not vote on whether the full 3rd Circuit should rehear the case. Three judges voted to have the full 3rd Circuit hear McIver’s case, and Judge Emil Bove, a former Trump administration official and former personal attorney for the president, did not participate in the vote.

The criminal case started shortly after the Delaney Hall visit in May 2025, as prosecutors alleged that McIver assaulted federal agents during a scuffle around Newark Mayor Ras Baraka. Officials arrested Baraka that day and charged him with trespassing, but later dropped those charges

Court filings in the case alleged that McIver struck agents during the confrontation. McIver has argued that she was effectively being charged for doing her job and federal agents were interfering with her attempts to inspect the facility.

Earlier this year, Judge Jamel K. Semper of the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey disagreed and ruled that the case could move forward.

#5932. How Washington Could Exploit Qatar’s LNG Shopping Spree

The U.S. may have a chance to drive a wedge between Doha and Tehran.

A tanker sails past ExxonMobil and QatarEnergy’s Golden Pass LNG facility in Port Arthur, Texas, April 2, 2026.

Brett Coomer/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images

America’s leading natural gas competitor is on track to become its biggest customer. With traffic down through the Strait of Hormuz, Qatar is betting on U.S. liquefied natural gas (LNG). The state’s energy company, QatarEnergy, signed two purchase agreements for American LNG in late October and is reportedly in talks with U.S. supplier Venture Global for a third. There may yet be more deals coming down the pike, including one with Houston-based NextDecade. QatarEnergy already owns 70 percent of Golden Pass LNG, a joint venture with ExxonMobil that shipped its first cargo out of Sabine Pass, Texas, in April.

Doha’s ventures are adding up. So much so that, according to an early November Financial Times report, Qatar may become “the biggest U.S. LNG buyer” by 2033. This presents the United States with opportunities to affirm market leadership and drive a wedge between Doha and Tehran.

Operating profit before finance costs fell 55.1% to 3.8 billion baht ($111 million), finance costs of 3.4 billion baht ($99 million) absorbed almost all of it, and one-time charges of 1.1 billion baht ($32 million) — mainly from flooding and currency losses — pushed the quarter into the red. Chief of finance and accounting Cherdchome Therdsteerasukdi said cost cutting, starting with fuel, is the priority for 2027, and warned that if current oil prices become "the new normal," the third quarter "could be a reference for Q4." Demand held up: the airline carried 3.97 million passengers at a 76.5% cabin factor, roughly level with a year earlier, and management said it would favor "proper profitability over aggressive volume." The loss lands during a leadership vacuum. The board suspended CEO Chai Eamsiri on Oct. 2 after Bangkok flooding crippled Suvarnabhumi operations, with a permanent successor expected by December.
