#5926. Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

Collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.

Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.

The amount of earmarks King secured fell dramatically compared to his previous year's total in Senate Appropriations Committee bills, as Collins took sole credit for most earmarks both senators had requested.

The power play has instigated a dispute over how to award credit for "congressionally directed spending," better known as earmarks. It has also raised questions about a Senate rule that requires committee leaders to disclose the name of each senator who requested projects to be included in a spending bill before it can move on the floor.

It’s undeniable that as the chair of the spending panel, Collins has more influence over which projects reach the final bills than her delegation mate. Collins spokesperson Phoebe Keller said that since available earmark funding is split into separate pots for the majority and minority to dole out, the bills reflect which of those funding sources was tapped to provide money to the relevant projects.

Keller said that Collins deserves sole credit for the contested projects, as listed in the reports accompanying the bills.

"When only Collins is listed, it reflects only she chose to fund the project,” Keller said.

A Democratic committee aide contested that characterization, saying that traditionally all requesters are named regardless of which party’s funding allocation is tapped for a project.

“The handling of these particular projects is a clear departure from the norm and will need to be rectified in conference negotiations,” the aide said.

King is credited with approximately $54 million in fiscal 2027 earmarks in the bills Collins released this month, including joint projects with Collins. That's down from around $231 million in the Senate's fiscal 2026 bills, according to a CQ Roll Call analysis.

Last year, King and Collins were both listed on 75 of the 77 projects that both requested that were included in the Senate bills, with just two carrying only Collins’ name. This year, Collins claimed sole responsibility for over $125 million in projects that both she and King requested, approximately two-thirds of the joint requests.

While King’s overall requests fell by more than $200 million this year versus last, his success in securing requested funds plummeted at a far greater rate with less credit for overlapping projects.

The joint requests for which Collins claimed sole credit include five for the Maine Department of Transportation in the Transportation-HUD bill, including $10.7 million for northern freight rail improvements; $9.6 million for Route 26 reconstruction in Oxford; and $7.2 million for improvements in Rockport, among others.

In the Labor-HHS-Education bill, projects Collins took sole credit for include $4 million for the University of Maine for biology laboratory equipment and just over $4 million for the creation of a modern emergency helipad at Lincoln Hospital.

And the Interior-Environment bill features $4 million each for wastewater improvements in Limestone and Kennebec that both Collins and King asked for but are only attributed to Collins, among others.

Similarly, the Agriculture, Commerce-Justice-Science and Homeland Security bills all include a project requested by both senators that only Collins is listed as securing in the bill.

The outgoing Appropriations chair’s ability to fuel billions of dollars in federal funding for her state during her career was the centerpiece of her ultimately unsuccessful campaign for reelection, which she lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.

As written, the draft bills appear to risk running afoul of a Senate rule that requires the committee’s chair to identify each senator who requested projects in a bill online at least 48 hours before a vote to advance the legislation on the floor.

The relevant rule, Senate Rule 44, states that it is out of order to vote on a motion to proceed to consider a bill unless the chairman of the committee certifies that “each congressionally directed spending item . . . has been identified through lists, charts, or other similar means including the name of each Senator who submitted a request to the committee for each item so identified.”

That information must be “available on a publicly accessible congressional website in a searchable format at least 48 hours before such vote.”

A King spokesman called on the spending panel to add his name to the relevant requests.

“We believe this must have been an oversight and assume the committee will update the requests —per Senate rules — once it’s called to their attention,” King spokesman Matthew Felling said.

The bills released by Collins are drafts, and no floor action on final fiscal 2027 spending bills is expected this Congress. There’s limited time left before the Dec. 11 spending deadline, when all current funding is set to expire, and Democrats want to wait to negotiate final bills until they retake majorities in both chambers next year.

But to comply with the rule, before the bills reach the floor the reports accompanying the bills, that includes the earmark tables, may have to be rewritten to list King on the contested projects, or the committee may need to disclose the information elsewhere online.

Both chambers unveiled stricter ethics guidelines surrounding earmarks in 2021 when the practice returned after a decade-long ban.

Pursuit Attractions and Hospitality, the Denver-based, NYSE-listed operator spun out of Viad at the end of 2024, is one of the few public companies that shows what experiential attractions actually earn. It runs the Banff Gondola, the Maligne Lake cruise, Sky Lagoon in Iceland, and lodges in several of the same markets, with Canada accounting for 54% of 2025 revenue. In the first nine months of 2026, visits to comparable attractions fell 3%, which the company attributed mainly to weather in Canada, but ticket revenue per visitor rose 7.5%, lifting ticket revenue 4.2%. Lodging is close to a second engine: in the peak third quarter, attractions brought in $131 million and hospitality $112 million, with comparable properties 92.3% full at $334 a night. Pursuit expects about $460 million in revenue and $126 million in adjusted EBITDA in 2026 excluding Flyover, the flying-theater business it sold in July. The cost side is where the test sits. Pursuit plans $103 million to $114 million in capital spending in 2026, operating cash after capital spending fell to $23 million through September from $56 million a year earlier, and a separate $300 million growth plan is expected to add more than $40 million in annual adjusted EBITDA by 2030. Safety obligations are also a cost: a fatality inquiry report released in October 2026 into the 2020 Columbia Icefield rollover identified brake failure and inadequate inspection, and Pursuit said it accepted all four recommendations.

#5922. Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

Showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohenâs latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses. âWho Is America?â The answer, on its face, will not surprise you: we are a nation of easy marks. Not merely easy, but willing.

Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of âDa Ali G Show.â His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.

Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom. But today, being on camera is so natural and desirable to most of us that we are willing to say or do just about anything for a few of the 15 minutes we believe to be our birthright.

âAli Gâ and the characters the show introduced, including Borat Sagdiyev and BrÃ¼no Gehard, also were born years before Project Veritas and InfoWars and other right-wing vehicles of disinformation made hidden camera hoaxing into something sinister.

All of which is to say, âWho Is America?â is not, as Showtime would like you to believe, âthe most dangerous show in history.â At best, it is an occasionally funny one.

But to anyone who mourns the collective deterioration of our populationâs capacity to engage in critical thought, but has no idea of how urgent of a crisis that happens to be, Baron Cohenâs new endeavor is less of a comedy than a fright show. âWho Is America?â A nation of pliable dullards ripe for the hacking.

âWho Is America?â was produced in secret, and its pre-show marketing largely consisted of publicized declarations of outrage by such right-wing figures as Joe Walsh, Sarah Palin and Roy Moore. Each attempted to transform their extreme embarrassment at having been duped by a British clown hiding behind layers of latex and spirit gum into some approximation of righteous anger at said comedianâs dishonesty.

Showtime, meanwhile, maintained the aura of mystery surrounding the series almost to the brink of its debut, revealing the title only a little more than a week prior. The network released the briefest of clips featuring one famous interview subject, Dick Cheney.

This in itself was a bit of flimflam Showtimeâs part: âHope youâll tune in next week for an interview with me,â Cheney says in the video, only to be a no-show in the premiere.

You canât blame âWho Is America?â for saving its biggest fish for later, because the famous politicians in the opener prove the problem of our collective gullibility just fine by themselves. In fact, although liberals may have gotten a hearty guffaw out of hearing Palinâs wailing about having been faked out by Baron Cohen, the very same characterÂ â Dr. Billy Wayne Ruddick Jr. PhD of Truthbrary.org â sat down for a conversation with none other than the honorable junior senator from Vermont, Bernie Sanders.

Prior to the premiere Billy Wayne tweeted a response to Palinâs accusation that he made fun disabled veterans. âI did NOT say I was a War Vet,â Ruddickâs âofficialâ response reads, going on to explain that the service was in was ânot military, but United Parcelâ.

Nor does he make such assertions to Sanders, with whom he debates the merits of a universal healthcare plan. And when I say debate, what I mean is that Sanders very calmly shares statistics with Billy Wayne long after the interviewerâs line of questioning stops making sense. And when Sanders asks Billy Wayne to confirm that he is disabled, given that he is conducting the interview while seated on a motorized scooter, Baron Cohenâs character replies that no, he is not. âThis here scooter is to preserve my bodyâs finite energy,â Billy Wayne says.

READ MORE: That viral âstrangers on a planeâ Twitter story: Not a rom-com but a horror show

One may be tempted to qualify Sandersâ appearance by pointing out that he acquitted himself well in the face of a person best be described as a few coconuts short of a beach vacation in Binomo.

But this fails to answer the question of why Sanders signed a release, allowing this interview to be broadcast. Did anyone on Sandersâ team vet Truthbrary.org the moment Billy Wayne mentioned it? Even if they thought he was genuine, what is to be gained from being seen in a televised debate with a guy whose site includes a page titled Â âObamanoids â For Real!â?

(To be fair, reportedly Baron Cohen almost fooled veteran news anchor Ted Koppel as part of his project. Koppel told The Hollywood Reporter that he was contacted to appear in a Showtime project titled âAge of Reason,â said to feature âconversations with distinguished experts in science and public policy, highlighting the brightest and most reputable minds on todayâs most important topics.â Koppel, perhaps receiving brainwaves from his colleague Sam Donaldson, wised up before Baron Cohen could pull him too deeply into his game.)

A second character introduced in the premiere, an NPR shirt-wearing hyper-liberal named Â Nira Cain-NâDegeocello, visits the opulent South Carolina home of wealthy Trump supporters he says are Â âafflicted with white privilege.â But it soon becomes clear that his marksâ problem isnât close-mindedness but over-correcting in the acceptance department. When Baron Cohenâs interviewer waxes on about encouraging his daughter Malala to âfree bleedâ on the American flag as a lesson, they simply nod and listen; when he chats about his wifeâs ongoing affair with a dolphin, they donât have any questions like, say, whether what theyâre hearing is real.

This brings us to another answer to âWho Is America?â: weâre so aware of cameras, and desperate to have its focus upon us, that we will do and say anything without thinking of its possible permanence.

Demonstrating this is Baron Cohenâs third character Rick Sherman, an ex-con turned TV host who visits a Laguna Beach, California gallery to show his work, which is a series of capable but otherwise unextraordinary portraits rendered in feces and ejaculate.

Now, itâs entirely possible that the woman who runs the gallery might have been thinking she could have the next Andres Serrano on her hands. On the other hand, please.

This is a subject entirely aware of being on view, so obsessed with appearing erudite that while Rick is off camera, having excused himself to the facilities to commit another brown-and-white vision to paper, she addresses the camera like the host she was born to be.

âWho knew the world was capable of such oxymoronic paradoxical juxtapositions?â she muses. And this is before the homemade pubic hair paintbrush comes out.

Baron Cohen has pushed the limits of tolerant everyday people many times in the past, mostly in a way that makes them look reasonable or, at the very least, more intelligent than the put-ons he inflicts upon them. And this is perhaps one of the most depressing aspects about âWho Is America?â, its demonstration of how endemic our lack of analysis truly is. Iâm not saying that gallery owner is a stupid woman, understand.

But her interview is an example of prizing exposure over lasting consequence. By that Iâm not merely referring to the fact that she placated a man who not only handed her pieces of cardboard purportedly smeared with his own dried excrement, or waited to receive a fresh sample of his work, but that she decided she needed to share her expert observation as to why she needed to do so by uttering a sentence full of five dollar words that add up to absolute nonsense.

(Either that or sheâs a friend of Baron Cohenâs and in on the gag. I hope itâs option two, as opposed to her actually legitimizing the artistic relevance of number two.)

A number of reviews of âWho Is America?â have pointed out that Baron Cohenâs sneaky deceit is no longer funny because the formerly insane viewpoints Baron Cohenâs tactics expose have been normalized.

This has always been the danger, but itâs one every sort of parody or satire contends with in the current climate. Itâs difficult to lampoon leaders seeking to legislate ludicrous patches to crises like gun violence instead of adopting common sense solutions like stricter regulation.

Which brings us to the portion of âWho Is America?â guaranteed to dominate Mondayâs gallery of crazy clips, fronted by Baron Cohenâs Col. Erran Morad, a self-styled Israeli anti-terrorism expert who calls himself âthe terrorist terminator.â

The fake Mossad officer is there to promote his âKinderguardiansâ program, a proposal that aims to train and arm toddlers in the classroom because, Moran says, arming teachers is crazy.

And this is the portion that has Walshâs boxers in a bunch, because he joins House representatives Dana Rohrabacher and Joe Wilson in lending on-camera endorsements. Walshâs comments are interwoven with a series of fake testimonials from the likes of Larry Pratt, executive director emeritus of the lobbying group Gun Owners of America and rape joke enthusiast.

Nobody forced Walsh to say, with gusto, âThe way to stop a bad guy with is a good child with a gun. Happy shooting, kids!â If he didnât want to say it, he wouldnât have.

What Walsh might be upset about is being upstaged by Pratt, who earns some of the episodeâs biggest laughs by reading the âscienceâ behind the effectiveness of the fake program, revealing he doesnât know the difference between human anatomy and hitmakers who grace Billboardâs pop charts.

Yes, âWho Is America?â gets mileage out of highlighting the callousness, sexism and extraordinary gullibility of conservatives, as Baron Cohen always has. But the things they say to him in disguise arenât all that different than what theyâd say on CNN, Fox, MSNBC or talk radio. Whatever power his comedy used to reveal is diminished by the fact that the charlatans no longer operate in secret.

Next weekâs episode introduces one or two new characters, although I donât imagine they do anything more âdangerousâ than the four we met on Sunday. For a number of viewers who love Baron Cohenâs schtick, that wonât matter.

To them âWho Is America?â is precisely on brand, showing Americans famous and everyday reacting to bizarre situations with varying degrees of what we consider to be normalcy in a time where the baseline version of normal is constantly morphing and shifting.

To other viewers, however, âWho Is America?â is a confirmation that Baron Cohen has run some tests and can confirm there is limited and ever decreasing brain activity in this worsening patient we know as America. It is something to behold, thatâs for sure. But Iâm not sure itâs the stuff of groundbreaking comedy. Itâs not even really news.

#5921. House Democrats eye stock trading ban as early priority next Congress

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, says banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the new year.

But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the issue could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.

“I’d rather have it be a clean bill focused on stock trading, and not muddy it by adding other topics, even if they’re good policies,” said Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I.

The incoming majority could plant a flag on government accountability with a broad package ranging from insider trading to campaign finance and more. Or they could zoom in on the stocks issue with a standalone bill.

Magaziner said he hasn’t received any assurances from House Democratic leaders, instead describing a “collaborative conversation” about what form the legislation could take.

“I worry that it would get weighed down under its own weight if you try to load it up with too many things,” Magaziner said, while stressing he would support whatever expected incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries decides.

Meanwhile, more than half of the Democrats in the incoming freshman class are calling for action on Day One of the new Congress, sending a letter to Jeffries last week suggesting they make a “down payment on much-needed reform” by changing House rules to curb stock trading.

“Democrats may have won the election, but we have a long way to go to earn back the trust of voters across the country,” reads the letter, led by Reps.-elect Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa and Jamie Ager of North Carolina. “A stock trading ban alone will not fix Washington, but it is the fastest way to show voters we heard them.”

Folding new language into the House’s internal rules would be a relatively easy path, requiring just a majority vote on the House floor, instead of passage in both chambers and the president’s signature. But such internal limits wouldn’t have the force of law, and some believe it would cool the urgency around the issue while doing little to crack down on insider trading.

Colorado Rep. Jason Crow said moving forward quickly with a rule change wouldn’t preclude passing a bill, suggesting his fellow Democrats do both.

“I want to pursue a parallel track,” said Crow, who co-chairs the End Corruption Caucus. “We want to move via rule and just prohibit it right out of the gate, or as much as we can.”

Jeffries has repeatedly said the topic is high on his to-do list as he looks to deliver on the accountability the “American people are demanding.”

“We’re committed to making sure we pass legislation that bans members of Congress from trading stocks. That will be a high priority,” he said at a news conference this week.

But with more than two dozen different bills on the topic introduced over the past few years alone, lawmakers will have to decide exactly what a “ban” means to them.

Some want to force members of Congress to fully offload their stocks with the exception of widely held mutual funds. Other proposals would block lawmakers from buying new stocks but allow them to keep the ones they already own, like a Republican-led bill that passed the House earlier this year but stalled in the Senate.

Democrats resisted that push, which was led by outgoing House Administration Chair Bryan Steil, R-Wis., partly because it included an unrelated voter ID provision they called a “poison pill.” Many also complained the measure didn’t go far enough, extending to members’ spouses and dependent children but leaving out key figures in other branches of government, such as the president.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., said she wants to stay close to the text of a consensus bill she hammered out last year with a small bipartisan group that included Magaziner and Reps. Chip Roy, R-Texas, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa.

“That is the most comprehensive, thorough, thoughtful proposal and bipartisan proposal that we have,” she said of the bill, dubbed the Restore Trust in Congress Act.

That measure would not apply to President Donald Trump, as many Democrats have urged as they seek to draw attention to his ballooning wealth while in office. Still, Jayapal suggested a presidential stock trading ban could be moved separately.

“There is discussion about the president, vice president, Cabinet, Supreme Court. I know we’re working on some language around enforcement, around those pieces, but I actually think that can be a separate bill,” Jayapal said. “We want to hold everyone accountable — but at minimum, we have to do ourselves.”

It’s not clear how much appetite will exist next year for a bipartisan compromise that could realistically clear a 60-vote cloture threshold in the Senate. Notably, key Republicans who worked on the consensus bill will be leaving Congress, with Roy losing a primary bid for Texas attorney general and Fitzpatrick unseated by a Democratic challenger.

While lawmakers could in theory advance a new stock-trading bill even sooner, before Democrats take control of both chambers, time and patience is short in the lame-duck session.

At a news conference at the Capitol earlier this week with Crow and Jayapal, a group of freshman and returning Democrats took matters into their own hands, promising not to hold or trade individual stocks as part of a broader pledge backed by the Political Integrity Project.

“My district, New York 10, happens to include Wall Street, but I don’t represent Wall Street. I represent the people of Brooklyn and Manhattan who deserve someone who goes to work every single day and shows right up front, ‘I work for you.’ And what better way to prove that than by day one showing we will ban members of Congress from enriching themselves, from trading stocks?” Rep.-elect Brad Lander said.

While momentum has grown in recent years as key senior lawmakers softened their resistance to a stock trading bill, not everyone is on board. Some members still argue, whether publicly or privately, that they should be able to trade on the stock market just like other citizens or that existing disclosure requirements established by a 2012 law are already enough to discourage dubious trades.

As they iron out the legislative text of any new bill, members will have to decide how to handle emerging topics such as prediction markets and crypto, along with sticky questions such as whether to allow blind trusts. And extending restrictions to the president could be a nonstarter for many Republicans.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said Democrats in the next Congress should look to a bipartisan bill that advanced out of the Senate Homeland and Governmental Affairs Committee in July 2025 as a model.

“The legislation we passed out of the committee applied to the executive branch,” he said. “But it didn’t take effect for anybody until their next terms, which was a compromise.”

That proposal would apply to future presidents but not the current one, potentially freeing up more Republicans to vote for it without angering Trump. Still, it hasn’t seen action on the Senate floor.

Hawley said that while he’d like to see a “full ban on trading and holding” in Congress, he would be open to a weaker proposal in the interest of getting something done.

“I’ll take anything that’s an incremental improvement over what we have now, which is nothing,” he said.

#5920. New Webinar: Who Remembers the Traveler? Building a Connected Customer Journey in the Age of AI

This sponsored content was created in collaboration with a Skift partner.

Travelers now pass through roughly 65 touchpoints before booking a trip, up from 45 in 2018, according to Skift Research and McKinsey. Travel brands own only a handful of them. Even within those, sales, booking, loyalty, and service run on separate systems, so the traveler’s history rarely follows them from one to the next.

That gap is getting more expensive. Personal AI assistants remember what travelers prefer, and they increasingly shape where trips begin. Agentic AI gives travel brands a way to compete: their own agents, carrying a traveler’s context from first search to the moment a trip is disrupted. Phil Wang and Ronen Kadosh of ElevenLabs join Skift to break down how customer experience leaders can build a relationship that remembers the traveler.

But then, the laugh-until-you-cry parts of the original âBoratâ donât involve, say, the Islamophobic, homophobic rodeo organizer mouthing off or those Southern frat boys wishing aloud that slavery was still legal. #5918. Will America Finally Confront the Massive Chinese Espionage Threat?

The Jensen Huang saga shows us that China’s spying is aggressive and ubiquitous.

Then-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang makes a keynote speech at Computex in Taipei, Taiwan, May 19, 2025.

Every few months, Washington rediscovers that China is spying on Americans en masse, expresses shock, and goes back to business as usual. And once again, it has happened. As a nation, we need to learn that our primary adversary is highly capable, extremely aggressive, and never lets morals or principles stand in its way. In other words, we must take the challenge posed by Chinese intelligence, cybersecurity, and influence seriously and protect ourselves accordingly.

According to widespread reporting this fall, U.S. intelligence concluded that a Chinese businesswoman who befriended Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang, while her company bought billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia AI chips was spying for China’s Ministry of State Security (MSS). Her Singapore-based firm reportedly began a multibillion-dollar purchase of Nvidia chips shortly after she was first photographed with Huang publicly. Her husband, Kang Wei, who originally introduced his wife to the Nvidia CEO, has in recent years built a massive data center empire with the overt support of the Chinese government. Of course, Nvidia says it complies with the law and has opened an internal investigation into the relationship. Beijing says that any claims about espionage are smears, as it always does. Huang, who had hidden this and other affairs from his board and colleagues, has resigned in disgrace but is now reported to be planning a comeback.

Then-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang makes a keynote speech at Computex in Taipei, Taiwan, May 19, 2025.

Expedia Group's B2B segment, the main driver of its recent growth, is set to slow after a quarter in which B2B gross bookings rose 19% and revenue rose 23%. On the November 4 earnings call, CFO Derek Andersen said growth would moderate in the fourth quarter, citing last year's heavy partner marketing that pushed Q4 2024 B2B gross bookings up 24% to $8.7 billion, softer demand tied to the U.S. election cycle, geopolitical disruptions in the Middle East and Europe affecting long-haul travel, and a fall sale that pulled bookings into Q3. Bernstein senior analyst Richard Clarke called B2B the weak spot in an otherwise strong quarter and told Skift four factors are at work: larger partners negotiating bigger revenue shares, lower-margin products such as flights and expanded services in the Travel Agent Affiliate Program, new competition from Booking Holdings' newly combined Booking Partner Division, and the tough year-over-year comparison. Margins are already moving: segment adjusted EBITDA rose 17% to $470 million while margin fell 134 basis points to 27.5%, which Expedia attributed mainly to partner mix and to investments including the Tiqets and CarTrawler acquisitions. B2B generated $1.71 billion of Expedia's $4.94 billion in Q3 revenue, while the consumer business grew gross bookings only 7%. Expedia declined to comment for this story.

This was somewhat surprising since Vance, one of the partyâs leading race-baiters, is married to the daughter of Indian immigrants, and Vivek Ramaswamy, another child of Indian immigrants, is Ohioâs Republican nominee for governor.Â

But none of these attacks and lies has gotten the traction they were hoping for, so the party has gone back to the deep well to draw up a big bucket of Islamophobia.Â

In the wake of 9/11, some in the GOP became infected by a strain of anti-Arab bigotry that, to his credit, George W. Bush attempted to fight. It waxed and waned as the attacks grew more distant. Then came Trump, whose demonization of Muslims goes back to the 2016 campaign. At that time, the U.S. was in the midst of an outbreak of âlone-wolfâ terrorist attacks, and his violent rhetoric really got the crowds going.Â

Trump famously said he wanted to take up waterboarding âand worse,â and told lurid stories about dipping bullets in pigs blood to scare terrorists. Declaring that he would ban all Muslims from coming to America âuntil we can figure out what the hell is going on,â he executed his infamous âMuslim banâ days after taking office in 2017, an order that became the focus of legal challenges and, after some re-tooling by the administration, was ultimately upheld by the Supreme Court in 2018.

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., has long been a particular focus of Trumpâs ire. As a progressive, she has been a fierce critic of the administration, but no more than most other Democrats. But sheâs a Black woman, an immigrant and a Muslim who wears a hijab. Omar, who fled Somalia with her family at eight and lived for years in a Kenyan refugee camp, represents Minnesota, which became one of Trumpâs bete noirs after Kamala Harris chose the stateâs governor, Tim Walz, as her running mate. Trump began attacking Minnesotaâs community of Somali Americans with some of the most bigoted comments in American history, and thatâs saying something.

Somalia, he said, is âgarbage, a âsh*thouse countryâ that âstinks.â He has even claimed that 98% of Somali immigrants donât work and that they are all criminals driving around in Mercedes-Benz and BMWs. Reprising his role as inciter-in-chief, the president called for (white) Minnesotans to âfight backâ against the stateâs Somali population, writing that they âview you as weak and stupid people.âÂ

Another target of MAGAâs anti-Muslim bigotry is Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan-born Democratic nominee for the Senate. Earlier this week, Vance referred to him as âvery, very evil,â a âpsychopathâ who pushes âanti-white racial hatred.â This charge of reverse racism is one of the favorite tropes of the modern right, guaranteed to draw cheers at a MAGA rally. Trump called El-Sayed a violent jihadist, and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. expanded the attacks, saying that the one billion Muslims worldwide contribute nothing to society, having never won the Nobel Prize or any other prestigious awards, an easily disprovable lie.Â

The blatant bigotry of these latest attacks is enough to take your breath away, not because they are unprecedented; this is America, after all, and racism is one of our âexceptionalâ characteristics. But until the last decade, Republicans had learned that it was far better for them to obscure their racism with dog whistles and code words so as not to scare the suburban white people.

But until the last decade, Republicans had learned that it was far better for them to obscure their racism with dog whistles and code words so as not to scare the suburban white people. The famous quote from the notorious GOP strategist Lee Atwater, who recommended referring to âwelfareâ and âbusingâ to stand in for overtly racist language, held true for years.

Republicans stuck with that tactic for decades, starting with Richard Nixon, who used the term Trump thinks he invented, âlaw and order,â as a code word for cracking down on Black protests in inner cities. Ronald Reagan famously talked about âwelfare queensâ during his 1976 primary bid for president, and four years later he opened his presidential campaign by declaring his belief in statesâ rights âÂ another dog whistle â in Mississippi, near the spot where white civil rights workers were killed. Three decades later, Trump turned even more creative with his âbirtherâ campaign against President Barack Obama, combining the partyâs burgeoning Islamophobia with classic All-American racism. To this day, Trump refers to Obama using his full name âÂ Barack Hussein Obama â with a childish glee.Â

I donât think claiming that a whole African country is a âsh*thouseâ or saying that Black immigrants are barbecuing their neighborsâ cats for dinner is the kind of subtlety Atwater was talking about. #5915. At the Races: The new Trump Democrats

Editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day. We’ll be back the following week.

By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari

Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.

Eight of those wins were in states that Donald Trump has carried every time he’s run so it’s no surprise that some of the incoming senators are talking up the prospect of working with him over the next two years.

“We don't have time to wait until we have a different administration in the White House,” South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews told reporters this week. “We have two years ahead of us. We have very real problems that we need to address.”

Andrews is the first Democrat elected to the Senate from South Carolina since 1998. A pediatrician, she cited reducing prescription drug costs as a potential area of common ground with Trump.

“I support the president's attempts to stop taxes on tips and taxes on Social Security,” Andrews said, citing two selling points of last year’s GOP reconciliation law. During the campaign, she issued a policy paper expressing support for making those provisions of the tax code permanent.

James Talarico, the incoming senator from Texas, told fellow Democrats gathered in Denver last week that if Trump wanted “the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality.”

“We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history,” said Talarico, the first Democrat in nearly 40 years to win a Senate race in the Lone Star State.

The idea of Trump and congressional Democrats working together might seem far-fetched, but with the incoming Democrats hailing from places such as Alaska, the Carolinas, Mississippi, Kansas and Texas, there’s a political incentive to appeal to Republican-leaning voters back home.

But intentionally or not, Talarico and other newly elected Democrats might be borrowing from the playbook of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has welcomed Trump when goals align, including on an effort to redevelop the Sunnyside rail yard in the president’s native Queens.

Trump has stressed that he will veto legislation he opposes from the incoming Democratic Congress, but, at least for the moment, he seems open to deals.

“I have a feeling that this is going to be an unbelievably productive two years,” Trump told Fox News early Thursday morning in Shenzhen, China, adding that  he would invite Democrats to the White House.

“I respect them,” he said. “Politics is a nasty game, and they won.”

Peltola prevails: Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s victory over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to 56 seats in the 120th Congress. Peltola finished with just over 50 percent of the vote, negating the need to use the state’s ranked choice voting system. The race for the state’s at-large House district was decided by a ranked choice tally, with Republican Rep. Nick Begich defeating independent Bill Hill 51 percent to 49 percent in the final round. Alaska voters also rejected an attempt to eliminate ranked choice voting in the state by a vote of 54 percent to 46 percent.

Leadership elections: House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries to serve as the next speaker in a 251-11 closed-door Wednesday vote, Roll Call’s Lauren Green reports. That puts Jeffries in prime position to become the first Black speaker when the full chamber votes in January. Meanwhile, Senate Democrats are scheduled to pick the next majority leader on Dec. 1, as our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports. Charles E. Schumer, who’s being challenged by Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen, maintains he has the votes to win.

A victory lap and a warning: Even as the Congressional Hispanic Caucus celebrates its largest roster ever, the group’s leaders had a warning for their fellow Democrats: “Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, who leads the group’s campaign arm.

#KYGOV: Republican Rep. James R. Comer, who was just elected to a sixth full term, launched his much-anticipated run for Kentucky governor this week. The Bluegrass State is one of three states holding statewide executive  elections in 2027, along with Louisiana and Mississippi.

Rocky Mountain roundup: Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken Republican with a national reputation as a Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for reelection in Colorado’s 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral. Meanwhile, Republican Gabe Evans, who fell short in his bid for a second term in the neighboring 8th District, announced he plans to challenge Laubacher in two years, Roll Call’s Samantha Freeman reports.

They’re back: Our colleague Nina Heller tracked down former congressional staffers who are back on the Hill as newly elected members. “I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” said Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, who worked for fellow Florida Republicans Greg Steube and Vern Buchanan, her soon-to-be House predecessor.

RIP: Former Rep. Jim McDermott, a longtime advocate for universal health care, died last week at the age of 89. The Washington Democrat, who retired to a small town in southwestern France after 28 years in the House, was hailed by his home state’s senior senator, Patty Murray, “as one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress.”

Where the House stands: As of 3 p.m. Eastern time, House Democrats have flipped 46 seats to three for the Republicans and are on track to hold at least 257 seats in the next Congress. Six races remain uncalled by The Associated Press, including two in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. The AP is also yet to call Tennessee’s 4th District, where Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais has conceded to Democrat Victoria Broderick, who leads by 272 votes out of nearly 200,000 cast.

Thompson loses: California Rep. Mike Thompson lost his bid for a 15th term to former venture capitalist Eric Jones, a political newcomer who poured millions into his campaign. Thompson is the second California member to lose to a fellow Democrat this year, after Rep. Jimmy Gomez. But Rep. Doris Matsui held off an intraparty challenge from democratic socialist Mai Vang.

2028 draft: Supporters of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg launched Team Pete PAC on Thursday, an effort to urge him to launch a second presidential bid.

Battleground rep: Michigan Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet will be House Democrats' battleground leadership representative in the next Congress, acting as a bridge between members in competitive districts and party leadership. McDonald Rivet, who ran unopposed for the position, will succeed Nevada Rep. Susie Lee.

#INGOV: Indiana Gov. Mike Braun launched his 2028 reelection campaign as speculation swirls that state Attorney General Todd Rokita could challenge him for the Republican nomination. Rokita, a former congressman, has criticized Braun for not disciplining state educators who posted controversial comments after Charlie Kirk’s assassination but said last week that he wanted Braun to “run for governor” and “be successful.” The two previously faced off in a 2018 Republican Senate primary, with Braun going on to serve one term in the Senate.

New leader for New Dems: Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski will chair the New Democrat Coalition next year, taking over from fellow Illinois Rep. Brad Schneider. New Mexico’s Gabe Vasquez, Ohio’s Greg Landsman and Washington’s Kim Schrier and Marilyn Strickland will serve as co-chairs of the center-left group, the largest ideological entity in the Democratic Caucus.

Remembering Holden: Former Pennsylvania Rep. Tim Holden, who served 10 terms in the House before losing a Democratic primary to Matt Cartwright in 2012, died Sunday at the age of 69. House members held a moment of silence for Holden on the floor Thursday. Republican Rep. Dan Meuser, whose district includes territory Holden once represented, described him as “well-liked and widely respected, including by those on both sides of the political aisle.”

Investigated: Ohio Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter is under investigation for alleged sexual harassment after the Democrat’s campaign hired a human resources firm to investigate the complaint. Both the Blue Dog PAC and the Congressional Progressive Caucus, which had endorsed Poindexter’s candidacy, dropped their support in the closing days of the campaign after learning of the allegation.

Tennessee two-step: Tennessee Democrat Jeri Green, who narrowly lost the open governor’s race to Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, announced a bid for the state Senate seat GOP Rep.-elect Brent Taylor is expected to vacate. Taylor narrowly defeated Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson in the redrawn 9th District, though both men were simultaneously reelected to their legislative seats.

The  historic “blue tsunami” that swept Democrats into commanding Senate and House majorities has some pundits questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again, observes Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections.

But you just have to look at the election results from two years ago to realize that when it comes to winning party coalitions, nothing is permanent anymore, Nathan writes.

Only the young: New York magazine catches up with young Republicans in South Carolina and finds that immigration policy and the war in Iran have turned many of the MAGA faithful against the GOP.

From satirist to senator: The Washington Post traces South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews’ journey from an online agitator who made relentless fun of Republicans to a newly elected senator who says she’s eager to work with her GOP colleagues.

Bad blood: The Boston Globe explores the long-standing rivalry between Maine’s two newest members of Congress: Democratic Sen.-elect Troy Jackson and Republican Rep.-elect Paul LePage.

Schumer’s choice: Uncertainty around whether Schumer will seek another term in 2028 has risen as the New York Democrat seeks to become Senate majority leader next year, Politico reports.

That's how long it's been since the Senate Democratic Caucus last saw a contested race for its top leadership position, with Maryland’s Van Hollen now challenging Schumer for the job.

After Democrats lost eight Senate seats (and their majority) in the 1994 Republican Revolution, 42-year old South Dakota Sen. Tom Daschle edged out Connecticut's Christopher J. Dodd by a single vote, 24-23, to succeed outgoing leader George Mitchell of Maine.

The last time a sitting Democratic Senate leader faced a formal challenge was a decade earlier, in 1984.

West Virginia's Robert C. Byrd, who’d been leading his party in the chamber since 1977, easily fended off a bid by Florida’s Lawton Chiles.

The last time either party experienced a contested race for the position was four years ago, when Florida Sen. Rick Scott challenged Republican leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky.

As Byrd did before him, McConnell handily defeated his challenger in the secret-ballot vote.

Machine recounts in a pair of House races in North Carolina are expected to be completed Monday. Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx trails Democrat Chuck Hubbard by 331 votes, while GOP Rep. Pat Harrigan leads Democratic challenger Ashley Bell by just over 2,500 votes. The trailing candidate could then request a partial hand recount.

Monday is also the deadline for Republican Rep. Brad Finstad to formally request a recount in his razor-thin race against Democrat Jake Johnson in Minnesota’s 1st District. Finstad, who reportedly said he’ll seek one, trails Johnson by 321 votes.

#5914. “Chaos” in the air: Five ways voting could be disrupted on Election Day

This article originally appeared on ProPublica.

As Americans head to the polls on Tuesday, voting experts are watching to see how the Trump administrationâs unprecedented efforts to assert more federal control over elections will play out.

Since President Donald Trump retook the White House, his administration has tried to force states to turn over their unredacted voter rolls and to restrict mail-in voting. The Department of Homeland Security has used its resources to identify and prosecute noncitizen voters, an effort that has unfolded alongside the agencyâs massive crackdown on immigrants.

The president has justified these steps by claiming, without evidence, that American elections are beset by fraud and that illegal voting is tipping the scales in favor of Democrats.

Courts have thwarted most of the administrationâs plans to date, but Trump and his top deputies have kept up the pressure. Most recently, theyâve threatened to prosecute election officials who donât reject ballots from people that the federal government has identified as likely noncitizens.

The administration hasnât explicitly ruled out sending federal agents to the polls or seizing ballots or voting machines.

Election experts say the cumulative effect has been to ramp up anxiety about the midterms and to erode votersâ trust in the system.

âThe administration has been creating a lot of noise, a lot of confusion, a lot of doubt,â said Ben Hovland, whom Trump fired as a commissioner for the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission earlier this year. He said he worries that this will make voters âsit it outâ and âthrow their hands up.â

In an emailed response to questions, a DHS spokesperson said Immigration and Customs Enforcement âis not planning operations targeting polling locations,â adding that the agency would only arrest people at the polls to address a safety threat as part of âintelligence-driven targeted enforcement.â

The DHS and the Justice Department âare laser focused on identifying, prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens,â the spokesperson added. âOur message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences â including criminal charges and deportation.â

Before and on Election Day, itâs typical for the major political parties to mount poll-watching operations, but both Democrats and Republicans say theyâve expanded these activities in this pressurized midterm.

Republicans will focus on issues such as voter eligibility and voter-roll accuracy, according to Ally Triolo, the Republican National Committeeâs election integrity communications director. Democrats will concentrate on voter intimidation and other hurdles to voting, Angelo FernÃ¡ndez HernÃ¡ndez, a Democratic National Committee spokesperson, said.

Here are five issues that voting rights experts say theyâre watching as this yearâs election unfolds:

An incident in Leon County, in the Florida Panhandle, illustrates the widespread anxiety about law enforcement at the polls.

Mark Earley, the countyâs supervisor of elections, told ProPublica he was âfuriousâ when two marked U.S. Customs and Border Protection vehicles parked outside the countyâs busiest early voting location last month, after heâd been repeatedly reassured by the administration that agents would not do this.

He reported the sighting to the FBI, then learned that the agents, who were headed out of state, had just stopped by to try to vote themselves. The episode generated a flurry of news coverage.

âGiven the negative media coverage regarding federal agents at the polls, it shows pretty bad judgment that they showed up in their official vehicles,â Earley said.

Itâs against the law for federal law enforcement to be near polling places.

Nick Brown, Washingtonâs attorney general, leads a group of Democratic state officials and voting rights advocates who have been planning how to respond if, indeed, there is real federal interference. The group has âwar-gamedâ how to react if government agents attempt to commandeer voting equipment or ballots.

âWeâve seen the tension and chaos thatâs in the air,â Brown said. He called the federal government âthe biggest challenge to smooth elections right now, which is not the way itâs supposed to be.â

A DOJ spokesperson said âthe best preparation for any election official is following federal law.â

Itâs routine for DOJ monitors to watch over polling places, and the agency has assured states that, in the midterms, its observers will follow the law and not interfere with voting or election administration. Still, state officials remain concerned. During Wyomingâs primary election, poll workers said they felt uneasy when DOJ monitors asked about their training and to inspect voting systems. The stateâs governor criticized these actions as âa bit aggressiveâ and âirregular.â

The Trump administrationâs multipronged effort targeting alleged noncitizen voters has already led to eligible voters being improperly removed from the rolls. Voting rights groups fear this will block some U.S. citizens from being able to vote when they show up on Tuesday.

Federal officials have made clear they plan to go after anyone they think is committing voter fraud.

On the first day of early voting in Texas, Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, posted a YouTube video announcing his intentions. âIf you violate federal election law,â he warned, âI will hunt you down and prosecute you.â

This threat came days after the DOJ sued California, seeking to block the state from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 voters it claims are âlikelyâ noncitizens. The administration had obtained the stateâs public voter rolls, which the DHS had blended with its own immigration information and third-party data.

In a court filing, California called the claim that there are 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls âspecious.â Los Angeles County analyzed a sampling of the likely noncitizen voters that the federal government claimed were registered there. Many werenât registered in the county or had never voted, the analysis showed. Some said on their voter registration forms that they were born in the United States.

Asked about the case, the DOJ told ProPublica, âFederal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections, and the Department has a duty to enforce it.â

A federal judge has rejected the DOJâs motion for an emergency order that would have barred California from counting the 20,000 votersâ ballots. (A federal appeals panel later backed that decision.) On Thursday, the administration sent grand jury subpoenas to California officials demanding records about their response to allegations of noncitizens on the stateâs rolls. Late Friday, a federal judge issued a restraining order blocking the DOJâs demands, calling them an âintimidation planâ that would interfere with legal voting.

Last week, the DOJ wrote a letter threatening to sue Washington state if officials there refused to review a list of 400 voters it believes to be noncitizens within 24 hours. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters late last month that the department was considering additional actions, saying there were âa number of states that weâre looking at.â

In a letter responding to the DOJ, Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs called the government list of 400 names ânot reliable,â saying it included U.S. citizens, people who arenât registered to vote and duplicate entries. âTime and time again,â Hobbs wrote, âDHS claims about noncitizen voter registration turn out to be greatly exaggerated or false.â

Sam Trepel is Rule of Law program director at States United Democracy Center and a former attorney for the DOJâs Civil Rights Division. She said the agencyâs actions involving California and Washington were a âdisturbing use of prosecutorial authority.â

Trepel worries that the DOJ may try to seize ballots cast by voters identified as likely noncitizens, before or after the election, which would âput their votes at risk and undermine trust more broadly.â

Voting rights advocates also worry that the governmentâs efforts to target noncitizen voters could frighten eligible voters to the point that they wonât show up.

A federal judge recently put limits on a multistate effort by the DHS to go door-to-door in search of suspected noncitizen voters, at least through Election Day, saying it was illegally intimidating legal voters.

âA voter could say, âWell, maybe I donât want to put myself on the target list here, maybe I wonât register, or maybe I wonât vote,ââ said David Janovsky, acting director of The Constitution Project at the watchdog group Project on Government Oversight.

States often change laws and rules related to voting.

Since 2024, Republican-led states have taken a number of steps that experts say will make it more difficult for some of their residents to cast ballots and have them count.

A North Carolina law, for example, requires voters to provide proof of identification when sending mail-in ballots. Under new rules, ballots now come with two envelopes, both of which must be sealed. Ballot rejections have skyrocketed, Democracy Docket reported, because voters arenât sealing the inner envelope.

Texas and other states have cut back on the number and location of polling places, especially in areas favoring Democrats. In hotly contested Tarrant County, which includes Fort Worth, the number of polling sites was slashed by almost a third. This could increase the risk of long lines and voter confusion on Election Day.

Voting rights groups such as the Texas Civil Rights Project are tracking two issues involving the stateâs voter registration systems. A software error at the Texas Department of Public Safety stopped several hundred thousand new voter registrations from being forwarded to local election officials, preventing them from being added to the rolls. A separate state system for updating registration information wasnât processing changes for several weeks, leading to more backlogs. Counties say theyâve been able to address these problems.

Every election features some issues with voting equipment.

So far, there have been isolated complaints involving touch-screen voting machines â including one from Dolly Partonâs sister in Tennessee â spawning fears that machines have been âriggedâ to switch votes.

ES&S, the company that makes the machines garnering the complaints, told ProPublica that the company hadnât received widespread reports. Election experts say occasional problems with touch-screen machines donât signify tampering or manipulation. Any attempt to tamper with programming would surface during testing by election officials and be corrected, they said.

Incidents in the run-up to the midterms have ratcheted up election officialsâ concerns about the potential for both cyber and physical attacks.

Last month, officials in several states, including Arizona, received envelopes with an unknown white powder. Arizona eventually deemed the material nontoxic, but Secretary of State Adrian Fontes said âthe fear it caused was real.â

In 2024, false bomb threats, thought to be from foreign actors, caused widespread evacuations of vote-counting sites across the country. The disruptions were brief, however, in part because a message board funded by the federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA, alerted election officials that the FBI had deemed the threats not credible.

Trump, however, has dismantled CISA since retaking the presidency, leaving states and local election officials to grapple with both physical and cyber threats on their own. Election nonprofits have stepped up to try to fill the gap, and states, with CISAâs help, have enhanced their own cyber defenses.

Derek Tisler, counsel and manager for the elections and government program at the Brennan Center for Justice, said the federal governmentâs absence has weakened the defenses.

âStates acting on their own just do not have the same power,â he said.

Election lawyers fear that actions by the Trump administration in the run-up to the midterms suggest the government will aggressively pursue postelection challenges if the results are not to the presidentâs liking.

Late last month, the DOJ sued Alaska, seeking to block the state from certifying the result of its Senate race if the Republican incumbent doesnât win. A federal judge threw out that lawsuit on Sunday, but the administration is expected to appeal.

Trump has said he personally ordered the lawsuit to be filed. It claims the system is unfairly rigged against Sen. Dan Sullivan, because another Alaska man named Dan Sullivan also qualified for the general election ballot. The New York Times reported last week that campaign aides to Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola orchestrated the candidacy of the second Dan Sullivan after a monthslong, statewide search to recruit someone with the same name.

Nonetheless, the DOJâs case is unusual, both because federal law prohibits the government from interfering with an active election and because challenges typically come after voting is complete. Postelection challenges are most often brought by losing candidates in state courts.

âThis is using the federal government to interfere with our election process in a way that I think is pretty troubling on multiple levels,â said Brown, the Washington attorney general.

In response to ProPublicaâs questions, the DOJ pointed to Blancheâs statement about the lawsuit on social media, which said the agency âdoes not seek to stop any ballot from being cast or to stop the certification of Alaskaâs election.â (The lawsuit calls it âvitalâ that the state not certify âany election result that may be impacted by voter confusionâ and asks the judge to prevent Alaska from doing this.)

Some election lawyers have suggested that if the GOP suffers significant losses, Trump could try to pressure Republicans in Congress to block new members from being seated. Several lawyers, including Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, say that the incoming Democratic majority would be able to fend off such an effort; courts, too, are likely to stymie it, though it might cause a short delay, according to Muller.

Brown said he and other attorneys general are also planning how to respond if local election officials or boards refuse to certify election results, based on their own claims of fraud or claims by the administration.

âI worry tremendously about what they might do,â Brown said.

#5913. Black voters could sway the midterms in surprising places

Loss aversion is a phenomenon in psychology and behavioral economics. Defined simply, it means that the pain experienced from a loss is felt twice as much as winning. In politics, that intensity manifests itself in motivation. If you take something away from people, they are going to feel it more acutely than promising them something, and the theft produces a backlash.

That’s what appears to be happening right now with Black voters. Across the country, they have been lining up to vote early, presumably against Donald Trump and the Republican Party’s MAGA agenda, in astonishing numbers, particularly in the South. That this comes only six months after the Supreme Court gutted the Voting Rights Act in Louisiana v. Callais should not come as a surprise.

In the Trump era, Republicans have become experienced at taking rights away from the American people. For women, it was the roll back of their constitutional rights when the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, sparking a backlash in that year’s midterm elections. Since Trump returned to office in January 2025, immigrants have come under assault from a xenophobic administration intent on carrying out mass deportations via masked, secret police rampaging through neighborhoods. The LGBTQ+ community, and trans people in particular, have seen their rights stripped away.

To many Black Americans, the GOP’s agenda and behavior will not have come as a surprise. After all, it’s been at the core of their history going back to before the country’s founding.

These policies have come as a shock to some Americans who never thought Trump would go there, and they have also opened the eyes of others to the cruelty at the heart of MAGA, overseen by the highest court of the land. But to many Black Americans, the GOP’s agenda and behavior will not have come as a surprise. After all, it’s been at the core of their history going back to before the country’s founding.

Black Americans know what it means to have their civil rights taken away from them. They understand fully the fear of being targeted by brutal, marauding gangs of armed men. In the decade following the Civil War and the passage of the 14th and 15th Amendments, Black people began to participate fully in civil society. Mississippi elected two Black U.S. senators and a lieutenant governor, and former slaves and their offspring enjoyed freedom of speech, movement and opportunity. But the white members of Southern society would not let that stand, and as soon as the federal government withdrew its troops, they stepped in with legal and social barriers to deny Black Americans their rights, this time backed by vigilante and state violence that became Jim and Jane Crow.

Almost a century had passed by the time Lyndon Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act in 1964 and the Voting Rights Act in 1965, a period characterized by subjugation and violence by the white majority. But Black America kept fighting, against all odds, until they won.

This year, we have seen yet another attempt by reactionary politicians and judges to turn back the clock. After the Callais decision, several Southern states reverted immediately to form and radically redrew their congressional districts to favor the white majority, making it much more difficult for voters to elect a Black federal and state representatives.

They may come to regret that decision. This isn’t 1955 (or 1855) anymore, as much as Donald Trump would like to make it so, and the Black community is once again mobilizing. According to experts, early voting data is showing something unexpected: The vote is being driven by young voters rather than just those who went through the earlier battles. It’s muscle memory for the Black community.

After 2024, when Trump won a surprising 15% of the Black vote — nearly doubling his share of 8% in the 2020 election — Republicans thought they were defying history to make great inroads within the community. Then, incredibly, the administration began attacking Black America. The result is what some politicos are calling a “Blacklash,” and it could very well be decisive in some places where nobody expected the Democrats to do well. And even if it doesn’t result in flipping seats, it’s a shot across the bow.

In Mississippi, prosecutor and former judge Scott Colom, who is Black, is running an excellent race against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, the GOP incumbent. Colom has made some very clever advertisements which have garnered a lot of national attention, but Republicans and Democrats alike had largely ignored the race until just a couple of months ago. Polling has tightened, and the GOP has dispatched an influx of luminaries, including Trump himself. For the first time in years, Democrats from Bill Clinton to Kamala Harris, along with a long line of senators, have descended on the state to support Colom. Former President Barack Obama even cut an ad for him. Mississippi has the largest population of Black voters of any state in the country. If Colum gets a big Black turnout with just enough disaffected whites, he could win.

Louisiana, after giving birth to the case that saw the Supreme Court’s conservative majority gut the Voting Rights Act, has been winnowed down to one majority Black district in a state that is one-third African-American. But there has been a surge in Black participation akin to what is seen in presidential years, which could prove decisive in a race for Louisiana’s open Senate seat that has been a sleeper until the last couple of weeks. According to a recent poll, Republican Julia Letlow and Democrat Jamie Davis are tied. Among voters who have already cast their ballot, Davis — who is Black — holds a six-point advantage, and 34% of early votes have been cast by Black Louisianans.

Then there’s South Carolina, which has seen Trump make three desperate appearances to shore up Darline Graham’s torpid campaign. The endangered incumbent, foisted upon South Carolina Republicans by the president himself following the sudden death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, is not getting the job done. As numbers cruncher Nate Silver pointed out, a recent New York Times poll showing the race essentially tied is not an outlier; she is in deep trouble. As of late October, the Times reports, “Black voters accounted for around 28 percent of early votes, while making up around 20 percent of the overall electorate in recent cycles. The trend is not unlike what we’re seeing in Georgia and North Carolina thus far.” If that holds true through Election Day, we could see the biggest upset of the whole campaign, largely due to Black South Carolinians saying “Enough is enough.”

In a few short hours, all the ads, mailers, signs and rallies will mercifully come to an end. I am cautiously optimistic, but like many, I’ll never celebrate prematurely again. There is good reason, though, to feel more positive than we have in a long time. Trump and his acolytes have overreached. Opting for the big tech credo of “move fast and break things,” they vastly overestimated their abilities — and the American people’s tolerance.

They have also aroused a group of Americans who know what it is to lose their rights and privileges. With all that history and so many battles, Black Americans have shown what it takes to never give up.
