#5912. Tom Petty and The Who box sets reveal two sides of rock history

Two great box sets being released for the holiday season from Tom Petty & the Heartbreakers and The Who showcase different approaches to exploring an artist’s back catalog with strong results on both sides. “Origins 1971-1978” chronicles not just the Heartbreakers’ first two albums but also documents the journey that brought them there, while “The Who By Numbers 50th Anniversary Edition” documents the band’s seventh album in a more traditional box set presentation. Both of the releases successfully accomplish their goals and deliver a worthwhile experience for interested listeners, but follow different paths to reach their respective sonic destinations.

“It’s not Tom Petty good.” That’s how Adria Petty described the standards against which decisions were made about what to include and not to include in the outtakes record. “Could this be any band? If so, it’s not in there . . . it’s gotta be something that really adds to the canon or we’re just detracting from the canon.”

In the case of the Petty box set, the records at its heart are the newly mixed and remastered editions of the first two albums: the eponymous first release and record number two, “You’re Gonna Get It!” Then there’s “Live from the Record Plant,” originally broadcast on KSAN-FM in 1977, a DVD of the band’s appearance on the BBC’s “Old Grey Whistle Test,” and finally (and most importantly for this release) a disc of unheard tracks: “No Sleep Til L.A.” and “The Cut Out Bin.” (On the LP edition of the box, the latter two are separate albums, but on the CD-only version, the two are consolidated.)

Rounding out the set is a Blu-Ray with hi-res stereo, Dolby Atmos and 5.1 immersive mixes, and importantly, a full-color 46-page “fanzine” called “Heart Attack” that serves as the liner notes for this box, with photographs, essays, interviews and commentary from members of the surviving Heartbreakers. There are other editions with additional advanced artifacts like posters or simulated Polaroids — my favorite is probably the “Punk to New Wave” trading cards — but if you’re in the target market for those kinds of fun treats, you’ve probably already ordered your copy.

What’s notable about the unreleased music featured on “No Sleep Til L.A.” and “The Cut Out Bin” is that it isn’t just a simple compilation of demos and rough takes in a logical order of some kind, but instead is deliberately curated into the shape of an album. It’s intended to convey the journey Petty and the band took to get to the place where they’re going into the studio to record that first record, capturing tracks from the Mudcrutch era (Petty’s pre-Heartbreakers band that also featured future Heartbreakers Mike Campbell and Benmont Tench) as early as 1971 and then as the Heartbreakers in their early days, learning to work in the studio in L.A. and in Tulsa, where their label Shelter Records sent them to learn how to make a record instead of running the meter on a L.A. studio.

The outtake record isn’t trying to fabricate something that doesn’t exist or inject fiction into the Heartbreakers legend, but rather, to show you how the band evolved from a bunch of kids in Florida who picked up and went out to L.A. to seek their rock ‘n’ roll fortunes on a wing and a prayer into a band that would end up being inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. It’s expanding the legacy, not rewriting history.

“It’s not Tom Petty good.” That’s how Adria Petty, who oversees Petty Legacy, the business concern that’s handling her late father’s catalog, told Salon as she described the standards against which decisions were made about what to include and not to include in the outtakes record. “Could this be any band? If so, it’s not in there . . . it’s gotta be something that really adds to the canon or we’re just detracting from the canon.”

And the collection absolutely burnishes the canon. It’s hard to listen to the selection of music and understand how any music business professional didn’t think this band had serious potential. There’s so many standout tracks: “Parade of Loons,” which opens the record, from the great rock ‘n’ roll tradition of writing a song from the perspective of watching the craziness unfolding around you is borderline new wave, but it also isn’t — it’s easy to understand why an industry struggling to understand the new guard needed to figure out where these new guys fit, exactly — and perusing some of the photos included in “Heart Attack” you can extend some grace on that front, because — as Adria Petty laughed, “These are not guys you want to date your daughter, you know?” But as you learn from some of the news clips included in the booklet, Petty did not want to be co-opted into anyone’s movement or limited by any genre.

“You’re Gonna Learn” is reggae-influenced at a time when that wasn’t a widely known, let alone embraced, genre in American rock, and they manage to pull it off without embarrassing themselves. “Up In Mississippi Tonight” could be an outtake from “Exile on Main Street.” There are also a couple of earnest and successful Dylan homages: “Wild Eyes” and “I Can’t Fight It.” If you’re going to borrow, borrow from the best (and from a guy you’re going to be on the road backing in 10 years).

Then there’s “Unheard Kind of Hero.” This is a song that Heartbreakers keyboardist Benmont Tench had previously mentioned as a song he saw the band perform before he was in it, and how he was astounded that a band in Gainesville, Florida, was writing original material like that. In “Heart Attack,” Tench offers, “I was following Mudcrutch around because they were so good, and they played a lot of really cool covers and they played some stuff of their own,” he remembers. And when he heard “Hero,” he asked a friend working for the band who sang it originally. When he was told it was an original, his reaction was, “OK, good lord. Because if you listen to that, whether he was 17 or 19 when he wrote it, the storytelling in it is the beginning.”

The box set is configured to bring the listener into the story, opening with the outtakes before taking you to the officially released albums, then live radio show and then, finally, the 1977 “Old Grey Whistle Test” performance. But I’d like to make the case that you should begin with the OGWT performance because it is utterly electrifying. Anglophiles are already familiar, but in case you’re not, the “Old Grey Whistle Test” is a legendary BBC music program that was the opposite to “Top of the Pops” in that its focus was on albums as opposed to hit singles. But this isn’t an OGWT where a band plays a couple of songs; this was one of their special editions where the band gets the full show. So this is a 40-minute performance by a band that was already famous and well-liked in the U.K., a status they were still fighting to achieve back home.

They’re dressed in black (Benmont Tench rocking a red shirt underneath his suit jacket), Petty looking more like a gunslinger, Ray-Ban aviators and studded guitar strap, Stan Lynch singing harmony vocals over Petty’s shoulder, Mike Campbell dropping guitar riffs and solos without breaking a sweat, Ron Blair sharing the center mic for harmony vocals but otherwise staying low-key back against the drum riser. It’s a time machine back to 1977, with camera work more evolved than we’re used to seeing because it was a TV show about music, not a variety show that featured a band. The colors are a little over-saturated, but people who are used to watching archival rock ‘n’ roll clips won’t be phased. The most jarring element is whenever the camera cuts to the audience, who look like they’d rather be anywhere else. A U.K. source shared that this was because this wasn’t an audience of Tom Petty fans but rather random people who’d put in for tickets and wouldn’t have been encouraged to be enthusiastic. Petty gets his revenge, though, at the last number. (No spoilers!)

The Who box sets are intended to be complete documents of individual records. So there’s the disc of the remastered album (which sounds fantastic), then the initial Townshend demos.

“The Who By Numbers” was released in 1975, but this is still being declared a 50th anniversary artifact. It features 92 unreleased audio tracks, a recording of the band live in Swansea in 1976, the requisite Atmos and stereo mixes, and a video of the full concert of The Who at the Silverdome in Pontiac, Michigan, in 1975.

Also included is what has become a trademark for the band’s reissue sets, a gorgeous full-color 100-page book of liner notes, interviews, lyrics, photographs and other assorted documentation. Even if you buy the CD box, you’re still getting the full-sized book because they put the CDs into an album-sized enclosure. The archivist this time is Andy Neill, one of the two names you want to see behind a Who reissue.

The Who box sets are intended to be complete documents of individual records. So there’s the disc of the remastered album (which sounds fantastic), then the initial Townshend demos. Townshend was approaching 30 when he began work on the songs for “By Numbers,” and he was in the middle of a number of personal dilemmas, as well as struggling with his and the band’s place within rock ‘n’ roll: “I felt detached from my own songs,” he confesses. He also rued the fact that he felt he owed his best material to the band, instead of being able to pursue more of a solo career, which all of his bandmates had done. Townshend’s “Who Came First” came out in 1972, but there hadn’t been anything since.

(Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images) The Who, 1975

The demos are lovely, ethereal sketches, documenting Townshend breathing life into his creations for the first time. There are two demos of “Keep Me Turning,” which didn’t make the cut and we wouldn’t hear until it appeared on “Rough Mix,” the warm and affectionate project he recorded with Ronnie Lane of the Faces two years later. A fun game is to take the Townshend demo of “Slip Kid,” where he’s kind of half-speaking, half-singing, and then compare it to Daltrey’s delivery on the finished version, which is the one song from this record that was built on the original demo. (This is a release that you’ll want the good headphones for.) The highlight is probably “How Many Friends,” which is the heartbreaker on the album; Daltrey’s read of it nails the pathos, but this version makes you wish that Pete maybe hung onto it for himself.

Up next is “Tracking Sessions,” which are initial loose takes with the whole band, but not finished vocals. It’s basically how the band taught themselves the new material, and it includes listings like “Ramport Jam” where they (sans Keith Moon, still making his way back to the U.K. after hanging out in L.A. and working on his solo record) fart around on a variety of instrumentals and a Faces song. This lasted about half an hour, but we’re getting only eight minutes; given the nature of the release, just give the fans the entire unedited mess. Throughout the sessions, you hear the band members making jokes and laughing; you hear Glyn Johns in the control room offering his thoughts; you hear Pete Townshend complaining about not being able to obtain a suitable breakfast. This stuff is gold.

Whereas the Tom Petty box set is intended to show you how they got to the first two albums, this release is trying to show you why this was the record between “Quadrophenia” and “Who Are You.”

There are also lovely early run-throughs of “Imagine A Man” with a solo Townshend on acoustic and Nicky Hopkins on piano, and similarly, “They Are All In Love” (a song that Daltrey did not initially want to sing) is also offered solo Pete. A prototype of “Blue Red and Gray” is here as well, thanks to Glyn Johns’ insistence: “I find that the hardest thing for me to do as a writer is to express optimism, general warmth and a feeling of good will to all men in a song,” Townshend said. “It feels trite and I hate it. That song, ‘I Love Every Minute Of The Day’ . . . is a prime example. Glyn Johns wanted it on the album; I cringed when he picked it. He heard it on a cassette and said, ‘What’s that?’ I said, ‘Nothing.’ He said, ‘No. Play it.’ I said, ‘Really, it’s nothing. Just me playing a ukulele.’ But he insisted on doing it. I said, ‘What? That fu*king thing. Here’s me, wanting to commit suicide, and you’re going to put that thing on the record’.”

Disc 4 is billed “Early Mixes & Guide Vocals” and is by nature more structured than the Tracking Sessions. The songs are taking shape now. Entwistle offers his approach to his “Success Story,” Pete sings the lead on “However Much I Booze,” there’s a version of “Squeezebox” that the liner notes state is “accented by tambourine” but sounds like the cowbell on the “SNL” “Don’t Fear The Reaper” sketch, and “Dreaming From The Waist” is a fantastic illustration of why Pete Townshend needed Roger Daltrey to sing most of his songs.

As a way to track the evolution of the song from start to finish, the inclusion of all of these different versions is an established and useful presentation device, but given their formative nature, it’s not likely that you’re going to go back to them with regularity. But that’s not why this record exists. Whereas the Tom Petty box set is intended to show you how they got to the first two albums, this release is trying to show you why this was the record between “Quadrophenia” and “Who Are You.”

But it’s probably more accurate to state that “The Who By Numbers” was the record between the “Tommy” movie and “Who Are You,” which isn’t a small distinction; the “Tommy” movie made the band into a larger and different flavor of rock star, one that brought in the girls because of shirtless golden god Daltrey and delivered your average punters who might not have found their way past the tunes they’d heard on the radio. And it’s not unimportant to note that the “Tommy” movie brought the band the kind of money they hadn’t yet seen.

That’s part of the cri de coeur you hear on “By Numbers.” It’s by no means the main thread, but it absolutely underpins Townshend’s personal anxieties. He’s annoyed that his bandmates are off doing their own thing. He’s perturbed that he doesn’t have the time or material to make another solo record because he has to offer his best songs to The Who (and conversely, it’s kind of hilarious that he then seems panicked when he presented Daltrey with the songs he’d written for the record and ended up shocked that Rog picked “the more personal ones”.) NOTE: Daltrey is not responsible for the abomination that is “Squeeze Box,” that we have to blame on Ronnie Lane, who was enchanted by it.

The Swansea show from 1976 here isn’t complete, but it is Keith Moon’s last proper show before a U.K. audience. (It was recorded with the intention of being released as a live album, and one of the original tapes went missing at some point in the 1990s, which is why the first two songs are missing.) “My Wife” will sound familiar to anyone who owns the “Maximum RnB” box set, “Squeezebox” is palatable because of Townshend’s giant power chords, “I’m Free” (introduced by Moon, who dedicates it to the occupants of the prison across the street from the venue) sounds more like the version from the “Tommy” soundtrack, and there’s a hilarious comedic bit over “Bellboy.”

But it’s the last live artifact here that’s a truly delightful surprise. It’s on the last disc with the Atmos remixes, and at first I feared it would be poor-quality footage added simply because it existed. But it’s far, far better than that. It is the complete show from the Pontiac Silverdome in December of 1975, cleaned up and remastered. This show set the record for the largest ever indoor rock concert attendance of 76,896, which would be broken by Led Zeppelin in the same place two years later. Because of the size of both the venue and the crowd, a large screen was set up to project closed-circuit video, a thing we’d think absolutely nothing of now, but at the time was a revolutionary development.

There were four cameras, and they do a more than decent job of capturing the action but don’t expect any fancy camerawork or closeups of guitar solos. The sound is in mono — as the liner notes point out, “the sound was captured via a direct line mono feed from the PA — no attempt was made to professionally record the concert for synching purposes.” Part of the “Join Together” / “Road Runner” / “My Generation” medley ended up in “The Kids Are Alright,” but this is the first official release of this footage.

You know what? The sound quality is more than adequate, and where it falls down the electricity coming off of that stage in this performance makes up for a multitude of sins. Roger is in Woodstock buckskin fringe, and even this primitive setup can capture that those trousers were, shall we say, form-fitting. (Wait for “Magic Bus,” which swings so much harder and better than it did later.) Daltrey introduces the “Tommy” portion by noting, “This is how we used to do it,” and then the band proceeds to light the stage on fire. The band seems perplexed and concerned about the size of the crowd, with both Roger and Pete each taking turns to ask the crowd to take a few steps back.

This Silverdome footage is absolutely a text, and even this rudimentary capture that was meant to make sure the 76,896th guy in the back could see something is still full of electricity and life. If you were lucky enough to see the band with Keith Moon in those days, you’ll remember, and if you weren’t, this at least brings some of that fairy dust into your life and your house. Put it on, turn it all the way up, and enjoy it without 76,896 people stepping on your feet.

#5911. House Ethics panel adopts changes aimed at speeding up investigations

Ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.

In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.

“My problem with the Ethics Committee is it just takes too damn long,” Rep. Madeleine Dean, D-Pa., said earlier this year.

The internal rule changes were adopted in a voice vote by the committee, which is evenly divided between Republicans and Democrats.

“We believe that these rule changes will provide more transparency. They will expedite our investigative process while maintaining protections for witnesses and victims, while also making sure that … due process is protected,” Chair Michael Guest, R-Miss., said during the meeting.

When former Reps. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., and Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, resigned earlier this year amid misconduct allegations, it sparked outrage as some called to rethink how the House polices bad behavior. Both men were on the radar of the Ethics Committee at the time, but such investigations have tended to move slowly.

“I want the Ethics Committee to move faster,” said panel member Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., back in April.

The committee did not immediately make available the exact text of the changes it adopted Thursday. But a summary sent in a news release earlier this week included one proposal aimed at “consolidating deadlines” for a member to respond to an investigative subcommittee’s findings. Another tweak aimed at speeding things up would give the chair and ranking member subpoena power on behalf of the committee, rather than requiring a full committee vote.

The summary described “codifying the Committee’s policy of publicly disclosing any findings that a Member engaged in sexual harassment or other sexual misconduct” while “prohibiting publication of the identity of any victim.”

Also on the list: “Expanding the circumstances under which fines and denials of privileges are considered an appropriate sanction to include any abuses of position.”

It comes as women on both sides of the aisle have formed a partnership aimed at reviewing how Congress deals with sexual misconduct and suggesting concrete ideas for an overhaul. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., has been co-leading that effort as the chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus alongside Republican Women’s Caucus head Kat Cammack, R-Fla.

According to Leger Fernández, the Ethics Committee has “consulted” with her group as it weighed the changes to its internal rules.

“The Ethics Committee was clearly listening to women staffers, and has been a great partner in our work. We appreciate how they’ve consulted DWC and that these proposals will improve transparency and help protect the identities of those who report alleged misconduct. Together with RWC, we will continue to work on additional legislation in our sexual misconduct reform agenda,” she said in a statement earlier this week.

Cammack said that, while “the entire system on Capitol Hill has been designed to create a chilling effect for victims,” the Ethics committee rule changes would help.

“Putting public disclosure of misconduct findings in writing, while protecting every victim’s identity, gives staffers a commitment they can count on. Faster investigations mean they get answers in time to matter,” Cammack said in a statement. “This is exactly the kind of change our bipartisan task force has been pushing for.”

Ethics ranking member Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., said everyone in the House should have “zero tolerance” for sexual harassment.

“We’ve worked very hard to look at ways that we could make the committee’s process fair, transparent and accountable, and I think we’ve done that,” he said at Thursday’s meeting.

#5910. Will the midterms live up to the hype? 6 key stories we’re watching

Across the country, voters are making their way to the polls in the climax of a vitriolic midterm election cycle set against the backdrop of an electorate souring on Donald Trump and Republicans. Inflation is up, consumer confidence is down, gas and diesel prices are through the roof, largely due to the president’s war of choice in Iran. The cruelty of his MAGA agenda has roiled the country and left a bad taste even in the mouths of some of his erstwhile supporters.

Each election is billed as being consequential; this one lives up to the hype. As we await the results, it’s worth taking note of several questions:

A tsunami, a trickle — or something in the middle? All are possible, but signs are pointing to significant Democratic gains, likely up to 25 seats in the House, as well as a Senate majority. Dr. Abdul El-Sayed looks increasingly likely to win in Michigan, and James Talarico has Democratic hopes up in Texas. Senate races in Maine, Kansas, Iowa and Alaska are in play, and it’s worth keeping an eye on South Carolina, Mississippi and Louisiana as well.

One sign will come at 6 p.m. when polls close in Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District, where Democrat Zach Dembo is facing off against Republican Ralph Alvarado. Once a Democratic stronghold, the seat went Republican in 2012 and, despite a close call in 2018, has remained in GOP hands since. Although the district has been gerrymandered to favor Republicans, the energy on the ground is with Dembo. If he posts and maintains a healthy lead, look for significant Democratic gains to unfold throughout the night.

What effect did redistricting have on the GOP’s chances?

The midterms will be the first test of the GOP’s redistricting strategy, which saw the party redraw congressional districts in Florida, Texas and other states, partly in response to the gains Trump made with Black and Latino voters in 2024. But polls show those margins have been largely erased as the electorate has turned on the president after nearly two tumultuous years in office, while Democratic legislatures in California and Virginia have imposed their own gerrymanders. According to a Politico poll, the GOP increasingly sees the coalition that returned Trump to office as “crumbling,” and may have gained little or nothing from all this adventurous map-drawing.

Will progressives be bolstered or chastened?

Losses — or even narrow wins — by progressive candidates could be used as more evidence by the party’s establishment wing of the need to tack toward the middle ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Larger wins would provide rocket fuel to the movement.

The size of the blue wave could well come to be seen as a measure of progressives’ influence and power within the Democratic Party. Losses — or even narrow wins — by progressive candidates could be used as more evidence by the party’s establishment wing of the need to tack toward the middle ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Larger wins — and victories in unexpected places, such as Michigan’s 7th Congressional District where William Lawrence, co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, stands a real chance of unseating incumbent Republican Tom Barrett — would provide rocket fuel to the movement.

Progressive groups are already on the offensive, getting a head start on spinning tonight’s election results, particularly in anticipation of a narrow El-Sayed win in Michigan. “Expect to hear narrow victories cited as evidence of weak electability,” a Progressive Change Campaign Committee memo obtained by Politico reads. “But a candidate’s first winning margin is not their electoral ceiling.”

Will the Haley Stevens drama matter in Michigan?

Haley Stevens, the Democratic congresswoman who narrowly lost to El-Sayed in Michigan’s Senate primary, has brought the drama in the race’s closing days. As late as Saturday night, she pledged to colleagues and friends that she was backing El-Sayed, only to turn up hours later at a church service with his Republican opponent Mike Rogers, and endorse the former congressman in a video. The cold-dish move has virtually drowned out El-Sayed’s closing message, with Stevens being formally kicked out of the Michigan Democratic Party.

The question now is if any of it will matter, especially in light of a New York Times/Siena poll taken before Stevens’ move that showed El-Sayed leading Rogers by 11 points. Michigan Republicans seem to think it won’t, telling Politico they wish the congresswoman had crossed the aisle earlier. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report agrees, moving the race in their ratings to “Leans Democratic,” a shift that was already in the works before Stevens detonated her bomb.

Still, the results in the state’s Democratic primary were far narrower than the polls showed, with El-Sayed besting Stevens by only 1%, or 14,893 votes.

The New York Times reported yesterday that the world’s first trillionaire has dropped a staggering $474 million this election cycle, an historic first. The amount has been spread out across a variety of groups, PACs and funds, but it doesn’t include the “dark-money donations” the Times reports he has also made. Most of the $168 million he contributed to the Senate Leadership Fund has served to shore up Ken Paxton, the GOP nominee for Senate in Texas, who is locked in a tight race with Talarico.

Musk has a lot riding on Tuesday’s results. Beyond the simple math of whether he got enough bang for his buck, there is also the issue of what will surely face him in the event of a Democratic congressional majority: investigations.

Musk has a lot riding on Tuesday’s results. Beyond the simple math of whether he got enough bang for his buck, there is also the issue of what will surely face him in the event of a Democratic congressional majority: investigations. If the blue wave materializes, Musk can expect congressional inquiries of his activities, including his reported interventions in Russia’s war against Ukraine and his leadership of DOGE during the early months of Trump’s second administration.

Each election brings surprises. Think not one but both of Georgia’s Senate seats going to Democrats in 2020, or Republicans making big gains in New York two years later.

This is the year we could hear the echo of Georgia’s 2020 election results in another Southern state. Despite boasting large Black populations, Senate seats in South Carolina, Mississippi and Louisiana have long been out of reach for Democrats. But there is now a path to victory for the party’s candidates in each of those states.

In South Carolina, the GOP incumbent Darline Graham, who was appointed to the seat at Donald Trump’s command following the death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, has proven to be a lackluster candidate, alarming even some Republicans with her performance in debates and on the stump. Democrat Annie Andrews has run a more nimble campaign, and between Graham’s performance and the national state of affairs, she appears to have narrowed the gap.

Mississippi’s incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith has also run a lazy campaign, expecting to coast to victory. But the national political environment under Trump, coupled with campaign gaffes, large Black turnout in the aftermath of the Supreme Court’s decision to gut the Voting Rights Act and clever campaigning by Scott Colom, her Democratic opponent, have helped to put the race in play.

Louisiana is also a wild card. The state, which is one-third African American, has also seen a surge in early voting among Black residents, and according to a recent poll, the race between Republican Julia Letlow and Democrat Jamie Davis, who is Black, is tied.

Polls are not predictive. The political history of these states continues to favor Republicans, but any of them could deliver one of 2026’s electoral surprises. If that happens, it will signal that the blue wave has become a blue tsunami.

#5908. The Public Interest Demands Free Speech for Broadcasters

The FCC has absurdly broad latitude to decide what political speech is permissible on the airwaves.

Federal Communications Commission Chairman Brendan Carr speaks during a press conference following an open meeting of the FCC in Washington, D.C., July 22, 2026.

President Trump makes no secret of his desire to punish broadcasters whose content he dislikes. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Chair Brendan Carr is a willing partner, going so far as to threaten the licenses of Disney-owned ABC stations with an early renewal proceeding. This highly unusual move (purportedly for unlawful discrimination) followed President Trump’s demand that ABC and NBC affiliates lose their broadcast licenses for unfavorable coverage of him.

How did we get to a point where the president and FCC chair can threaten a broadcaster’s license over disfavored content? Two features of federal law enable this abuse: a vague public interest standard open to broad, subjective interpretation, and an archaic equal time rule.

Brian A. Rankin is an adjunct fellow with the Competitive Enterprise Institute.

On “The Public Interest Demands Free Speech for Broadcasters”

#5907. MAGA panics as post-midterm investigation season looms

Among all the gruesome details of allegations both old and new of rape and sexual abuse, there’s one four-word phrase in the new congressional report on Jeffrey Epstein that says a lot about why Donald Trump seems especially unhinged these days: “No statute of limitations.” Led by Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee released their findings on the president’s long and close relationship with the deceased sex offender. The report, citing testimony from 11 women, “indicates that Trump abused, assaulted, and even raped numerous women alongside, and in coordination with, the most infamous sex trafficker in history.”

The media response to the allegations was muted, despite compelling new evidence about the extent of Epstein’s sex trafficking ring, suggesting more powerful men were involved than have faced legal repercussions. Perhaps the report was overshadowed by the midterm elections. Or maybe there’s a sense this is “old news” and won’t move the needle. But if Raskin has his way, we’ll all look back to this release as the opening chapter in a season of accountability not just for Trump, but also for various administration figures and MAGA cronies who have enjoyed the legal shield of a Republican congressional majority.

Democrats are expected to win control of the House, and perhaps even the Senate, in the midterm elections. If they do, they’ll have access to a lot more power to investigate not just Trump and the White House, but also various Republican donors, right-wing business interests and other MAGA-aligned power players.

Democrats are expected to win control of the House, and perhaps even the Senate, in the midterm elections. If they do, Raskin and investigators will have a lot more power to investigate not just Trump and the White House, but also various Republican donors, right-wing business interests and other MAGA-aligned power players who have been taking full advantage of the atmosphere of corruption the president has created. The Epstein report is likely just the beginning. As the Washington Post noted on Monday, Democrats “are laying the groundwork for an array of inquiries into President Donald Trump, his family and his administration.” Various business and political leaders are meeting with their lawyers, worried about what Democrats could uncover with this new power.

“I haven’t seen this much investigative activity in anticipation of a change in control of a house of Congress ever,” Michael Bopp, who runs a congressional investigations division for the law firm Gibson Dunn, told the Post.

There are plenty of signs that it’s dawning on people around Trump that he will be out of office in two short years and that, as the latest Epstein report indicates, the statute of limitations has not run out on many possible crimes committed under the White House’s protection. A recent Zeteo profile of Stephen Miller showed that the White House deputy chief of staff is worried about going to prison if a Democrat wins the presidency in 2028. Congressional Democrats keep talking about impeaching Pete Hegseth, and the defense secretary is clearly anxious, reportedly making calls and begging Sen. Marsha Blackburn to appoint him to her Senate seat if, as expected, she wins the Tennessee governor’s race this week. Having a Senate seat would not only prevent impeachment; it could make prosecuting him for alleged war crimes much harder as well.

In October Elissa Slotkin of Michigan set off a massive panic on the right when she suggested that there should be a focus on “signature cases” against “people who enabled” Trump. The Michigan senator wanted a “deterrence message” for anyone considering working for Trump, letting them know that committing crimes or otherwise assisting in illegal or corrupt activity might result in “a ton of problems” for them that aren’t worth the risk of legal liability. Fox News and other outlets tried to spin this as Slotkin threatening the mass arrest of young staffers, but the hysteria belies their real worry: Democrats might be able to compile enough evidence that prison is a real threat for many of the people working for Trump.

Slotkin’s remarks clearly rattled the White House. Since then, Trump has repeatedly put out word that his underlings should not have to worry about obeying the law because mass pardons are on their way. A few days after Slotkin’s warning, sources inside the White House told the Washington Sun that administration lawyers are looking at “blanket pardons for all employees involved in particular policy areas, such as deportations, war or trade.”

Still, the White House is facing serious staffing issues. A September report from the Partnership for Public Service found that people Trump hires quickly leave. Not only have there been a record number of resignations, nearly half of the quitters worked less than a year for Trump.

On Monday, Trump himself also told the New York Post that widespread pardons are on the table, not just for his staff, but for allies like Tesla CEO Elon Musk. Musk has good reason to be worried. His brief tenure running DOGE has raised a whole host of questions about what laws were broken by him or by staff carrying out his orders. He’s also under suspicion of messing with Ukraine’s Starlink access, crippling its defenses against the invading Russian military. This may explain why Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars — more than any single donor in history — trying to tilt the elections in the GOP’s favor.

Trump and his family members should also be sweating. Trump has often interpreted the Supreme Court’s grant of presidential immunity as all-encompassing, but as Raskin told the New Yorker, he doesn’t see it that way at all. He outlined how the president has made billions in office, roughly $1 million a hour, and that there’s a great deal to learn about where that money is coming from. The Supreme Court’s decision technically only covers crimes committed during the commission of official presidential duties. By definition, Trump’s external money-making enterprises aren’t that. His children are deeply involved in the family business as well. And as the Epstein report made sure to note, some of the crimes Trump and his associates have been accused of committing with his old friend Epstein carry no statute of limitations.

It’s tempting to wave all this off as inconsequential, because Trump and his cronies were able to escape severe ramifications the last time around. But to dismiss this talk would be a mistake, in no small part because Democrats need their feet held to the fire. The corruption this time around is far worse than it was in Trump’s first term, more flagrant as the air of lawlessness led to a level of carelessness that creates more prosecutable evidence. The next Democrat in office may not be like Joe Biden, who shied away from aggressive prosecution of Trump and his allies. Some of the politicians whose names are being bandied around — like Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York or Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia — have been highly focused weeding out MAGA corruption.

Then there’s the matter of political will. Before now, it was hard to drum up sufficient political support for accountability because voters simply didn’t care enough about corruption. But as the New York Times reported last week, the issue is a rising source concern for voters. Democrats, for one thing, are doing a better job of linking Trump’s self-dealing to the economic problems of ordinary people. For another, the Epstein scandal has broken into national consciousness, and even Republicans are struggling to sufficiently explain why Trump, despite signing a bill to release all Justice Department files related to the case, is refusing to do so.

With these winds at their back, Democrats have a much better chance of being able to conduct thorough investigations — and pursue criminal consequences for those found to have broken the law.

#5905. Iran resolution blocked in first war powers vote since midterms

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., seen here at the Capitol on June 17, said additional war powers votes are under discussion for when Democrats control both chambers in the 120th Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The Senate rejected a resolution Thursday meant to rebuke President Donald Trump over the Iran war weeks after the midterm elections demonstrated the depth of public anger about the war and its effects on the U.S. economy.

Senators voted 48-51 against adopting the Iran war powers resolution that the House previously adopted in mid-September that would direct the president to withdraw U.S. forces from the war.

As they have previously with similar measures, GOP Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky broke with their party to support the resolution, while Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania broke with his party to oppose it. Departing GOP Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who have at times voted in support of similar measures, this time voted against the resolution.

Even if the resolution was adopted in both chambers of Congress, it would be largely symbolic since, as a concurrent resolution, it would not go to the president for his signature.

But the vote afforded senators the opportunity to register their complaints about the war for the first time since Democrats routed Republicans in the midterm elections.

It also comes amid a larger debate within the Democratic Party on how best to fulfill their campaign promise of ending the war as they prepare to take control of Congress next year.

Democrats have become increasingly interested in trying to cut off funding for the war rather than continuing to hold war powers votes. But they are divided on whether to demand an immediate end to funding in the next government funding bill in December or to wait until they take power in January.

“When we have the gavels, we are contemplating other things, and we're actually contemplating things in connection with the CR discussion,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., told reporters Thursday in an apparent reference to the debate among Democrats.

As of Nov. 13, the war has cost at least $48.3 billion, up from $47 billion last month, the nominee to be Navy comptroller, Arthur Miller, told the Senate Armed Services Committee at his confirmation hearing Thursday.

As with previous estimates, the number Miller cited Thursday includes munitions, equipment replacement costs and operational costs but does not factor in the cost of damage to U.S. bases, which alone is likely to run in the billions.

Last week, a trio of Senate Democrats unveiled legislation to prohibit funding for offensive military operations in Iran that they said they intend to introduce as an amendment to the next government funding bill, which Congress will need to pass to avoid a government shutdown after Dec. 11.

On Thursday as the Senate voted on the war powers resolution, Sens. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., and Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., two of the sponsors of the proposed amendment, demanded it be included in the next funding bill.

“We’ve already tried tool after tool to get the president to rein in this conflict. Nine months in, defunding the war is the only way to force Trump to end it,” Duckworth, who vowed to vote against any continuing resolution that doesn’t include the amendment, said at a news conference.

Sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., unveiled his own proposed amendment Thursday to bar any future and previous funding from being used to “support directly or indirectly combat activities by United States personnel in or over Iran, or in Iranian territorial waters” unless specifically authorized by Congress.

His legislation is modeled off of language Congress passed in 1973 to cut off funding for the Nixon administration’s bombing campaign in Cambodia, Bennet’s office said in a news release.

“When we vote on short-term spending in the near future, we can fund the government and end this war. It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve,” Bennet said in a statement.

Meanwhile, the House is likely to vote again on a war powers resolution before year’s end.

“Before the lame duck’s over, I hope to enforce a war powers resolution vote, and it’ll be a chance for Republicans to say whether they did or didn’t get the message on Nov. 3,” Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., said Thursday in a brief interview, referring to the date of the elections.

As with previous resolutions, Massie’s would direct the president to remove U.S. military units from hostilities against Iran unless specifically authorized by Congress or needed to defend against an imminent attack.

The resolution was filed Nov. 10, and under the 1973 War Powers Resolution, Massie can force a vote 15 calendar days after its introduction.

John M. Donnelly and Lauren Green contributed to this report.

Trump, however, insisted the network’s coverage of him was responsible.

“They’re way down, not because of me, but because they are AGAINST me!” he wrote. “This happened once before, and Fox almost collapsed. It’s happening again!”

#5903. The Gulf Is America’s Next AI Security Test

Analysis: The Gulf Is America’s Next AI Security Test

In the wake of Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation as CEO of Nvidia over his alleged affair with a Chinese spy, the U.S. Commerce Department this week announced new export controls on artificial intelligence and semiconductors. These rules mark the most serious effort to close the loopholes that have allowed Chinese companies to obtain access to U.S. chips and computing power. The new interim rules target three vulnerabilities: Chinese rerouting of U.S.-made AI chips through third countries, rented access to AI computing power, and Chinese chip designers’ ability to manufacture advanced chips at non-Chinese facilities.

The Nvidia scandal—including the alleged rerouting of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China and the Trump administration’s apparent quiescence—underscores the scope of the Chinese threat to U.S. artificial intelligence technology. The new rules close important gaps, but they do not resolve the threat. The next area where the United States is especially exposed is the Gulf, where the most advanced U.S. chips are now arriving, to be utilized in data centers operated by partners that maintain extensive ties with China.

In the wake of Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation as CEO of Nvidia over his alleged affair with a Chinese spy, the U.S. Commerce Department this week announced new export controls on artificial intelligence and semiconductors. These rules mark the most serious effort to close the loopholes that have allowed Chinese companies to obtain access to U.S. chips and computing power. The new interim rules target three vulnerabilities: Chinese rerouting of U.S.-made AI chips through third countries, rented access to AI computing power, and Chinese chip designers’ ability to manufacture advanced chips at non-Chinese facilities.

The Nvidia scandal—including the alleged rerouting of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China and the Trump administration’s apparent quiescence—underscores the scope of the Chinese threat to U.S. artificial intelligence technology. The new rules close important gaps, but they do not resolve the threat. The next area where the United States is especially exposed is the Gulf, where the most advanced U.S. chips are now arriving, to be utilized in data centers operated by partners that maintain extensive ties with China.

The Gulf magnifies the Nvidia problem. Both the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia are trying to shift their economies away from oil, and they’re placing AI at the center of their strategies. In May 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump announced that both countries would be able to purchase advanced U.S. chips to help facilitate these efforts. Abu Dhabi and Riyadh are financing massive AI buildouts, where Nvidia chips will be installed, operated, and even rented to customers or cloud tenants. The two monarchies are taking advantage of their desert land areas, access to lower-cost energy, and deep coffers, offering Nvidia an appealing market and affording Washington an opportunity to keep U.S. technology at the center of the AI buildout.

Both the Saudis and the Emiratis, however, also maintain deep relations with China. Washington fears that Beijing could gain access, intentional or not, through its contractors or cloud customers—or via hardware or software that may be connected to U.S. systems or chips. Chinese infiltration could occur through a trusted partner, with or without their knowledge, without directly acquiring the restricted chips.

That’s why companies such as the UAE’s Group 42 have caught the eye of China watchers and technology hawks. The group’s past links to China and its tech sector, even though the company publicly renounced them after the Biden administration declared it a security risk, raise questions that diplomatic assurances cannot resolve. The issue is not what the company says but whether its operations, ownership, partnerships, and access to sensitive technology can be independently verified and insulated from possible Chinese exploitation.

Saudi Arabia presents a similar challenge. The kingdom is pursuing AI autonomy by seeking control over every layer of the technology stack. But Washington will want evidence that Saudi officials can protect their data centers and cloud services from unauthorized access. And that case is increasingly difficult to make as Saudi Arabia continues to partner with both U.S. and Chinese technology companies.

The new rules make the Gulf an important litmus test for whether Washington can enforce its new approach in third-country data centers. Gulf-based facilities will need to prevent restricted users from accessing compute power enabled by U.S. chips, including indirectly through the cloud or other intermediaries. It’s not just about whether a Chinese company or user can rent compute power through a Gulf partner, but also whether the safeguards are in place for partners who maintain U.S. compute power to verify ownership and the affiliations of users.

U.S. export controls were designed for trade in tangible goods, but the Commerce Department has now acknowledged that simply controlling the physical movement of chips is not enough. The new rules extend export controls to some forms of remote access and computing power—intended, for example, to prevent a Chinese company from renting access to a processor through a data center or cloud provider. The new rule is a major step forward but not a complete solution. Safeguarding U.S. chips will require more than protecting the physical product or regulating direct access. It will require oversight of the people and systems that can use the computing power that those chips provide. That means guarding not just the chips’ physical location but also their ownership, network architecture, and consumer access.

Instead of determining which country or firm is purchasing a chip, an export policy will need to ask who will own and operate the facility, who can administer the compute power, which customers can rent its processors, what the networking and software infrastructure is made of, the nationality of users, and even whether the systems can be accessed outside of where they are housed. A processor being utilized in a Gulf data center, for example, may be used to provide computing power to a restricted Chinese company or state institution through the cloud—so controls must follow the user, not just the export.

Nvidia sells the most advanced chips in the business. Its former CEO, who made himself the face of the company’s strategy and government relations, was close with Trump and has decried more stringent export controls on AI chips, arguing that such restrictions will merely move more consumers toward Chinese suppliers like Huawei. His influence may have helped persuade Trump to sell limited amounts of the H200 chip to China. But the concern extends beyond Huang’s influence. Questions about the administration’s handling of the policy—including conflicts of interest involving U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Trump’s own financial interests in Nvidia, and other relationships between U.S. officials and companies that may have benefited from certain sales, like Jared Kushner’s—warrant a review of these decisions. Regulators should begin by reexamining the decision to allow the sale of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to Saudi Arabia and the UAE.

A new oversight policy would not entail a crackdown on Nvidia or a blanket ban on selling further advanced chips to Gulf states. Instead, Washington would expand access only when Gulf states meet specific conditions and establish guidelines for continuously evaluating who can access the technology. The new framework should become the baseline for future Gulf licenses that can identify approved facilities and consumers; limit chip quantities and aggregate compute power; prohibit restricted access and rentals; and require oversight of inventories, access logs, and control standards. Washington should also retain the right to suspend a license at any time. China has already sought to lease capacity through data centers in Europe and accessed U.S. chips to train its models through systems in Thailand.

When the Democrats take control of the U.S. Congress in January, they will likely press for tougher oversight of foreign chip deals—as they should. Democrats and Republicans have a considerable opportunity to work together on this issue. Even though this week’s new rules help address some of the areas of concern, they are an executive branch policy and thus subject to change at any moment. Congress can focus on passing the Remote Access Security Act, which will require export policy to include remote access controls, and the AI Overwatch Act, which will give Congress more oversight over foreign chip sales.

For the UAE and Saudi Arabia, access to the most advanced chips is still possible but now comes with stronger U.S. demands—and any failure to adhere to those conditions should mean that access is immediately cut off. Fair or not, the Nvidia scandal raises the cost of assuming that trust is enough protection.

However, tighter U.S. restrictions also carry some risk. If U.S. requirements become too stringent, intrusive, costly, or unpredictable, Gulf governments may turn back toward Chinese tech or tilt toward other suppliers with fewer restrictions. Greater reliance on Chinese tech would not replace the U.S. technological edge overnight but over the long term, it could well reduce U.S. influence.

The UAE and Saudi Arabia are seeking slightly different things. The UAE is leading the space in dealmaking and pushing the next generation of AI models, while Saudi Arabia is seeking to build out local compute capacity. For both, ongoing relationships with Chinese tech companies will remain an issue, and Washington will need stringent controls and verifications on who can access and use the systems.

China’s challenge to U.S. AI is a serious threat, and the United States must strengthen its technological defenses in the Gulf and elsewhere. The Commerce Department’s new rules are a meaningful step in closing the regulatory gap in U.S. export policy on chips. The Saudis’ and Emiratis’ AI ambitions make them key tests of whether the United States can enforce this approach. That requires systematic and continuous scrutiny of many more layers of the AI value chain than current U.S. export controls offer, including ownership, users, infrastructure, and remote access. The Saudis and Emiratis will, of course, say that they can be trusted. But in the post-Huang AI space, it is simply too risky to rely on assurances alone.

#5902. Jon Ossoff projected to handily win reelection in Georgia

Sen. Jon Ossoff easily defeated a challenge from Republican Rep. Mike Collins to hold on to his Georgia Senate seat on Tuesday, according to AP projections.

After Donald Trump carried the state in 2024, early forecasts predicted tough sledding for Ossoff. But during a brutal government shutdown — the longest on record — the senator signaled he was willing to stake his candidacy on protecting Affordable Care Act subsidies, and he proved an adept campaigner who was hyper-focused on Georgia issues. Ossoff focused his stump speeches around affordability, skyrocketing inflation and foreign entanglements, hammering Trump for his costly war with Iran.

For his part, Collins’ candidacy was hamstrung by controversies involving his payroll and affiliation with alleged white nationalists.

Frequently floated as a 2028 contender, Ossoff adopted a fighter’s stance at his campaign events. Like feisty Michigan candidate Abdul El-Sayed, the senator took every opportunity to land a jab against Republicans, occasionally causing some monocle-popping among centrist commentators still holding on to the idea of the dignity of the presidential office. In August, he drew jeers and applause for making light of the rumors surrounding Trump aide Natalie Harp.

“So [Trump] doesn’t want to do this job,” Ossoff said . “He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar.”

Ossoff, for his part, has said he has “zero interest in running for president.” His victory speech, which will come later tonight, will be studied by pundits seeking to divine his intentions.

#5901. Keisha Lance Bottoms set to become first Black woman governor in US

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated Republican billionaire Rick Jackson in Georgia‘s gubernatorial election Tuesday, becoming the first Black woman elected governor in American history and ending more than two decades of Republican control of the state’s highest office.

The contest pitted two sharply different candidates to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Brian Kemp, whose departure opened the governor’s office for the first time in eight years.

Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor and adviser to President Joe Biden, campaigned on expanding access to health care, improving public education and addressing the rising cost of living. Jackson, a billionaire health care executive and political newcomer, emphasized cutting taxes, reducing government spending and bringing his private-sector experience to state government.

Jackson invested more than $200 million of his own money into the campaign, making his bid one of the most expensive self-funded gubernatorial campaigns in American history.

The election also ended Republicans’ decades-long control of Georgia’s governorship. The last Democrat elected governor was Roy Barnes in 1998. Barnes lost his reelection bid to Republican Sonny Perdue in 2002, and Republicans have held the office since Perdue took office in January 2003.

Georgia’s changing political landscape added another dimension to the contest. Once a reliably Republican state in presidential elections, Georgia narrowly backed Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 before returning to President Donald Trump in 2024. Democrats also captured both U.S. Senate seats in 2021, with Raphael Warnock subsequently winning a full term in 2022.

On Tuesday, Georgia voters also reelected Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, demonstrating the state’s continued willingness to support Democrats in statewide contests.

Bottoms is the first Black governor elected in Georgia, the first woman to hold the state’s highest office and the first Black woman elected governor anywhere in the United States. She is also the first Democrat to win Georgia’s governorship in 28 years, breaking a Republican winning streak dating back to 2002.

#5900. Andrews defeats Graham in South Carolina Senate shocker

Dr. Annie Andrews will be the first Democratic senator from South Carolina since 1998, according to AP projections. In a stunning upset, she defeated the incumbent Republican Darline Graham, who was hand-picked by Donald Trump to succeed her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, following his death in July.

A pediatrician, Andrews positioned herself as an antidote to Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s MAHA agenda. Her campaign launch video hinged on measles outbreaks and the harm of anti-vax sentiments at the highest levels of public health. She described Kennedy as the “brain worm guy” and slammed Trump’s Cabinet as uniquely unsuited to their positions.

The race was never supposed to be close. South Carolina is about as red as you can imagine. The haven of cheap gas and fireworks hasn’t elected any Democrat to statewide office since 2006. Trump carried the state by 17 points in 2024.

Unlike her sibling, who shifted from staunch Trump critic to late-in-life ally, Graham was joined at the hip to the Trump administration from the outset. The president’s high disapproval ratings worked to turn the typical GOP lay-up into a closely contested race.

But Graham, a novice politician, did herself no favors. She flubbed softball questions around foreign affairs on the debate stage, a strong suit of her hawkish brother. Her dismal poll numbers pushed Trump to rally for Graham repeatedly in the state, cementing even stronger associations between the Republican nominee and Trump’s unpopular policies.

High early turnout among Black voters in the state also spelled trouble for Graham. The community, which is largely Democratic, turned out in high relative numbers and helped swing the race toward Andrews.

The Democratic candidate worked to avoid the associations with national party leaders that hamstrung Graham, refraining from appearances with prominent Democrats in the race’s final weeks. Andrews painted herself as a pragmatist, willing to work with national Republicans to score wins for South Carolinians. Late last month, Andrews received a shocking bipartisan endorsement from two former governors of South Carolina. Republican David Beasley joined Democrat Jim Hodges to support Andrews over Trump-backed Graham, saying Andrews was the only candidate focused on “making things better.”

#5899. Is This the Beginning of the End for Modi?

Analysis: Is This the Beginning of the End for Modi?

Thousands took to the streets in New Delhi last month to protest irregularities in electoral rolls and alleged election fraud. Reports claimed that more than 130 million voters were deleted from electoral lists, in ways that would benefit Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). But will this anger in New Delhi spread to the rest of the country, weakening Modi’s 12-year hold on power, or will it simply fizzle out as time passes and other concerns become urgent?

A lot depends on India’s opposition parties and whether they can keep up the momentum until elections in 2029 and offer a viable alternative to the people—but equally on how the populace rates Modi’s performance. Has he raised their standard of living? Is the opposition right in alleging that the BJP is systematically hollowing out Indian democracy? Increasingly, those questions are being answered in a way that makes it seem like Modi has peaked.

Thousands took to the streets in New Delhi last month to protest irregularities in electoral rolls and alleged election fraud. Reports claimed that more than 130 million voters were deleted from electoral lists, in ways that would benefit Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). But will this anger in New Delhi spread to the rest of the country, weakening Modi’s 12-year hold on power, or will it simply fizzle out as time passes and other concerns become urgent?

A lot depends on India’s opposition parties and whether they can keep up the momentum until elections in 2029 and offer a viable alternative to the people—but equally on how the populace rates Modi’s performance. Has he raised their standard of living? Is the opposition right in alleging that the BJP is systematically hollowing out Indian democracy? Increasingly, those questions are being answered in a way that makes it seem like Modi has peaked.

At a Diwali party last month, a young Indian researcher in her mid-20s warned me against attending a protest rally. “The police will pick you up,” she said, her eyes wide open. In a recent protest, the Delhi police had locked down major parts of the capital and cracked down on protesters. The police cut off the internet, shut down local trains in key areas, and detained thousands, including journalists. Even those hanging around weren’t spared. “Our lawyer friends who went to the protest site to help the protesters were also beaten up,” she said. “Because our friends were detained and beaten, now we fear we could be next. You could be next.”

This is starkly different from India in 2011, when tens of thousands flocked to Jantar Mantar, a historical protest site near Delhi’s power center, for an anti-corruption demonstration. That protest paved the way for the Congress-led government’s defeat and Modi’s entry into national politics in 2014. Modi’s government, however, appears to have drawn a very different lesson about how to deal with protests.

BJP leaders suggested removing protesters because they inconvenienced passersby and businesses. That line was parroted relentlessly in TV studios. In my travels in and around Delhi, I found that message landed with certain people—mostly those who also believed the BJP’s insinuation, which came without any evidence, that protests in India were a foreign ploy to destabilize the country. Protests in India unfolded at the same time as in France and elsewhere in Europe, and this was portrayed as a sign of collaboration.

However, there appears to be a pattern in how the current Indian government discredits and responds to protests. A few months ago, when Indian students marched against an exam paper leak and jobless growth, the same police thrashed the students, even firing pellet guns. Some TV anchors claimed the police were the victims.

These are unusual scenes in India, a democratic country where the right to protest is guaranteed under the constitution. India won its independence through peaceful protests against the British.

On Nov. 1, despite the police’s reported highhandedness, thousands of people from different parts of the country gathered for the mega protest at an alternative and government-approved protest site. By noon, as I reached Connaught Place in central Delhi, Congress workers were marching on the streets and calling for the removal of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. They accused Kumar of working to benefit the BJP.

But Kumar’s role and the discrepancies in electoral rolls weren’t the only reasons that pushed people to protest. Three Gen Z protesters stood in a corner, two of them wearing masks to avoid being identified by the police. “They picked up people after the protests last time, from their homes,” said one of the masked boys. All three had joined the protests for very different reasons but the same cause—saving Indian democracy.

The masked boy recounted the story of how his friend, a child, was terrified for his mother’s security when Hindu-Muslim riots unfolded in Delhi early 2020. He blamed the BJP for instigating the riots. The young man standing to his left hailed from West Bengal and was furious that his grandparents, both octogenarians, were knocked off the voters list and denied the right to cast their ballot. “[The government] wanted to exclude a certain community, Bengali Muslims that they falsely say are Bangladeshis, but everyone was affected,” he said. “They are dividing us on the basis of religion; this is not okay.”

Mihika Omseema refused to cover up her face. She said her parents supported her and that gave her the strength to reveal her identity and take part in protests. She said she joined to protest against growing Hindu-Muslim polarization, falling economic standards, exam paper leaks, and a whole host of other issues. In Delhi, some neighborhoods showed a mood where parents might join their children—if not at the protest grounds, then at the ballot. A senior gentleman and an upper-caste Hindu said, “Modi will not win Delhi, no chance,” but he confessed that Modi still had many supporters in the country. An 80-kilometer ride to Meerut has been shortened from more than 3 hours to less than 2 hours via a new flyover completed under Modi’s government, which has also built several other key highways linking cities in western Uttar Pradesh. Meerut, for the first time, has a fast train that reaches Delhi in less than an hour and thus expands employment potential. (Uttar Pradesh has the maximum number of electoral constituencies and plays a decisive role in forming the government in Delhi. Although central elections are still more than two years away, the state itself will go to the polls next year.)

In Meerut, I heard a different set of complaints against the BJP. Younger people acknowledged infrastructure development but said there was still no work. Only Muslims were worried about growing polarization; Hindus were more upset with slow economic growth and a demolition drive to bulldoze illegal shops and other structures. “Of course, this will affect the BJP in the elections; people are, we are, very angry with the government,” said Aditya Kumar, who sat on a stool in his emptied and recently destroyed shop in a market where rubble had still not been cleared. He sold nuts, bolts, and other construction material. “The structures were illegal, but there is no other employment, so what were we supposed to do?” he said, highlighting the lack of industry and compulsion to resort to small retail businesses.

“This is dictatorship,” said Kumar, a staunch Modi supporter until the demolition drive. “And no one raises our voice because the media doesn’t broadcast anything critical of Modi.”

About a dozen other upper-caste Hindus in the city who professed to be pro-Modi said the BJP was unlikely to win Meerut even if it retains the state. That could change if there were credible opposition, but they did not see a match. Congress scion Rahul Gandhi marched alongside protesters and promised to seek justice for those wrongfully detained or beaten up. In Delhi, Gen Z protesters spoke in his favor. But in a state deeply divided along caste lines, despite being upper caste, he is still not seen as an alternative.

Akash, a 26-year-old from Bulandshahr, said that the BJP will return to power because it had ensured quick payment for sugarcane to farmers like his father. “There are also more roads and police stations,” he said, emphasizing improvement in law and order under the BJP government led by Modi acolyte Yogi Adityanath. He said that Indians like him would rate Modi on economic development over the protests in Delhi or the state of Indian democracy. But he also didn’t want to give up his own right to protest or question the government.

“If the choice is between a better economy and democracy, I choose the economy, but if it is between the economy and my ability to question the government, then I choose democracy,” he said.

Like Meerut in Uttar Pradesh, in the Shekhawati region of Rajasthan, local factors were adding to a sense that all was not well under the Modi government. But here, too, the protests were not the reason that people said the government could change. “Farmers are not being paid on time,” Bhawani Singh, a tourist taxi driver, said. “Our children will never go and protest like those in Delhi. But we are upset about the Agnipath scheme and the shortening of military service,” he said, referring to government plans to cut down the length of service below the rank of officer to four years and retain only a quarter for a full term. “Most kids here want to join the army or the police,” he said. (The government appears to have noticed the grievance, announcing earlier this month that two more years of service could be offered and a second chance at joining longer-term,, for those who meet the selection criteria.)

Local factors remain paramount for Indians deciding how Modi has fared in his third term. The protests have had some effect on their overall assessment—distancing those affected by other government policies, while many remain ambivalent or supportive. The weakening of institutions isn’t yet a factor in how they vote, but it has been registered, as former supporters say the media is largely pliable, and now the Election Commission is suspected of being subservient.

The fence-sitters are the upper-caste Hindus who form the backbone of the BJP’s voter base. And while many are still firmly behind the party and backing Hindu dominance, at least some appeared uncomfortable with a slide away from democracy. “He wants to be Putin,” an upper-caste Hindu said  . “Now with the delimitation bill, the BJP is trying to ensure it always has enough seats to keep them in power,” he added, referring to legislation that will come up for voting in parliament next month and intends to expand the number of seats based on population. The same exercise in Jammu and Kashmir, Chief Minister Omar Abdullah said, helped the BJP.

The recent protests are occurring in the middle of Modi’s current stint in office. He still has time to assuage concerns. But the opposition will also have a chance to highlight its case about the weakening of democratic institutions and the threat to Indian democracy. And just as a political wave pushed Modi into office 12 years ago, another one could be building that will eventually sweep him out.

#5898. Van Hollen: Senate rules changes a matter for caucus to decide

Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore. looks on as Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., during a press conference on Thursday. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., endorsed a bipartisan plan Thursday to adopt new rules aimed at speeding up Senate procedures but stopped short of calling for abolishing the filibuster, laying down a marker on a key internal debate for Democrats as he positions himself to challenge Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

Van Hollen joined Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., at a press conference Thursday to express his support for a plan from Merkley and Sen. Steve Daines, R-Mont., to, among other changes, adopt a “talking filibuster,” requiring senators to continuously hold the floor if they seek to prevent a bill or nomination from moving forward.

Van Hollen went further to say that while his personal view is that the filibuster itself is “anti-democratic,” changes beyond what Merkley and Daines are proposing are a matter for further discussion.

“I’m in favor of filibuster reform,” Van Hollen said. “How and when we do that is a matter for the caucus to decide.”

The filibuster, a Senate tactic that effectively requires a 60-vote threshold to advance most legislation, has long been the subject of calls for change or outright abolition from members of both parties.

Other changes Merkley and Daines unveiled in October include eliminating cloture requirements for nominations and amendments, reducing post-cloture time for legislation, and introducing a new suspension process modeled after the House rules to allow bills with broad support to move quickly.

Merkley actually held two separate press conferences Thursday on his filibuster proposal, one with his Montana Republican co-sponsor and then later with Van Hollen, whose bid to become majority leader he has endorsed.

At the earlier appearance, Daines said that he thought the changes, if adopted, would “truly be a cultural change for the Senate” and lead to greater bipartisanship.

“We believe these reforms are appropriate no matter who is in the majority, no matter what the election outcomes were,” Daines said.

Daines also reiterated his view that implementing any rules changes would require 67 votes from the full chamber.

But Democrats have been debating whether to use their new majority in 2027 to change the rules on the first day of the session with 51 votes, or to eventually employ the so-called “nuclear option,” a series of procedural moves leading to a simple majority vote.

Democrats used that tool in 2013 to lower the voting threshold for advancing some presidential nominations with a simple majority, rather than 60 votes. A Republican majority followed in 2017 by extending that change to include Supreme Court nominations, and again in 2019 to reduce the number of hours between a cloture and final confirmation vote.

A spokesperson for Schumer declined to comment on Van Hollen’s endorsement of the Merkley-Daines plan.

Schumer has said he remains confident in his bid to remain party leader.

Van Hollen reiterated Thursday that his “momentum is growing,” after several senators-elect have thrown their support behind the Maryland Democrat.

“I think people recognize that if we're going to deliver on the big things that the American voters stood up for and voted for, you can't just go back to business as usual and status quo,” Van Hollen said.

#5897. Talarico, Hinojosa win big in Texas despite Elon Musk’s millions

James Talarico, the charismatic Texas state representative who campaigned by talking extensively about his Christian faith, has defeated state Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was Donald Trump’s hand-picked choice, in Tuesday’s most high-profile U.S. Senate race. Late on Tuesday evening, Talarico led by more than a million votes, and the Associated Press called the race just before 11 p.m. Eastern time.

This marks the first time a Democrat has won a statewide race in Texas since 1994, and another such result, perhaps even more surprising, followed almost immediately. Democrat Gina Hinojosa has won the Texas governor’s race, according to the AP, beating Republican incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott by more than 700,000 votes.

The big blue wave of 2026 has featured numerous surprising results, including the upset victory by Democrat Annie Andrews over Republican Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina’s Senate race. But these dramatic and unexpected Democratic wins in Texas stand out. The Senate campaign between Talarico and Paxton became one of the most expensive state-level races in American history, and according to CNN analyst David Axelrod, Hinojosa was outspent 10 to one by Abbott. Talarico’s campaign also became a major target for Democratic donors and an opportunity to vent their frustration and anger with Trump’s second presidential term.

A combined $573 million were spent by Talarico and Paxton, as well as their defeated primary opponents, over the course of this campaign. Much of that spending was the result of Elon Musk, the world’s richest man. The CEO of SpaceX and Tesla pumped an estimated $474 million into this race, virtually all of it to support Paxton, setting a new record for a single donor in a political campaign. Most of that money was funneled through went to Musk’s personal super PAC, but around $168 million went to the Senate Leadership Fund. Another $10 million went to the pro-Paxton Lone Star Liberty PAC, which spammed voters with AI-generated robocalls attacking Talarico. Meanwhile, Talarico’s campaign and Democratic PACs raised about $133 million.

Although Talarico, like other Democrats, focused on affordability and fighting corruption, he also sought to challenge the dominant view that only Republicans can be devout Christians. His campaign attracted various right-wing conspiracy theories, including claims that he was an emasculated “secret vegan” who suffered from mental illness. Democrats worried that this viral misinformation might overshadow numerous allegations about Paxton, including a Wall Street Journal report that he partied in Dubai with two fugitives from U.S. justice and a woman who wasn’t his wife.

Although Talarico has led in recent public polls, the size of his victory was unexpected. At this writing, it appears almost certain that Democrats will win the Senate, having already flipped seats in both South Carolina and North Carolina, where former Gov. Roy Cooper easily won the open seat held by outgoing Republican Sen. Thom Tillis. Democrats also lead the Senate races in Iowa, Maine and Ohio, although those races remain undecided.
